item.content:encoded:
♿️ The Week’s News in Access Information

Access Information News. The world’s #1 online resource for current news and trends in access information.

A Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. Publication

Subscribers:  47,294 🔢️ opt-in subscribers were sent this issue via email.

Social Media:  199,512 🔢️ readers were sent this issue via social media, courtesy of the PWD Media Distribution Co-Op.

Share: Facebook | X (Twitter) | LinkedIn | Email | Web Link | How to read this newsletter if you are blind or low-vision.

Section Jumper: Sponsors | Access Awareness | Featured Advertisement | News | Featured Events | Classified Ads | Supporters | News Team | Subscription Information

Sponsors 🏅️

Access Awareness: Updates That Matter ♿️

I Blindfolded My Fiancé For 24 Hours | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | August 25, 2026

For a 24-hour empathy experiment, Molly Burke blindfolds her fiance and documents how he navigates a day without sight. The challenge puts everyday routines at the center of a conversation about accessibility, independence, and the assumptions sighted people can bring to daily life.

This Week’s Featured Advertisement ️

Sponsorship Packages Currently Available: Join Industry Leaders in Supporting Free Access Information News For Disabled Readers All Over The World While Increasing Traffic To Your Properties Each Week. Advertise in every issue. Or just one.

Join Access Information News as a Sponsor today and begin reaching over 45,000 access information readers each week, all while supporting the ongoing distribution of Access Information News for those very same readers. Only $200 / month.

Key Newsletter Statistics:

  • Subscribers: 45,000 + per week and growing.
  • Open Rate: 47% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Click Rate: 34% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Bounce Rate: 1.2% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Ad CTRs: 2-12% (Average. Last 12 months.)

Benefits All Sponsors Receive:

  • One (1) Sponsor Profile on the Access Information News website, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Profile in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement on the Access Information News home page + every page of the website (Right Side Bar: Sponsors), for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Classified Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Membership in the PWD Media Co-Op, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • 50% Discount on all Sponsored News Article Advertisements, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Free link tracking, for all time.
  • Permanent SEO benefits. (All Sponsor Profiles are archived on the Access Information News website at the close of Sponsorship. Driving traffic back to your properties for all time.
  • Gratitude from over 45,000 blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled professionals, educators, and enthusiasts, all over the world, along with the caregivers, companies and organizations that serve and support them, for keeping Access Information News free to read each week.

With additional benefits for Sponsors who choose to pay quarterly or annually. Learn more about Sponsorship today. today.

News 📰️

👉 Submit a news article for free here, with timing and placement determined by our editors.

👉 Submit a Sponsored News Article here, with timing and placement determined by you.

1.) Top 5 Most Clicked News Articles From Last Week 📊️

A.) Contributor: Stop Shaming the Use of AI. For Some With Disabilities, It’s a Godsend | LATimes.com | August 20, 2026

Sharon Schindel challenges blanket condemnations of AI writing tools, arguing that for people with physical disabilities, AI can provide critical accessibility. She describes dictating her work due to severe arm pain and using AI only to clean up transcription debris, not to generate content. Schindel notes that 1 in 4 U.S. adults have a disability and stresses that universal prohibitions on AI risk excluding many voices.

B.) Call Luna. Learn Anything: Meet Derek Fine and Luna AI, Now Sponsoring Access Information News | AccessInformationNews.com | August 24, 2026

Luna AI, founded by Derek Fine in January 2026, enables users to access an AI tutor by simply calling +1 (231) 879-5862, requiring no app, account, or screen interaction. The phone-based conversational AI offers spoken study sessions using both general and user-uploaded materials, and remains free to use as of August 2026. Fine, with a background in travel marketing, plans a paid Luna AI Pro tier in 2027 but currently operates Luna solo as an early-stage project.

C.) Hikers Who Use Wheelchairs Explore the Outdoors, Watching Out for One Another | DisabilityScoop.com | August 21, 2026

Oregon Wheelchair Hiking, founded in 2020 by Franklin Ouchida, has grown from four friends to a Facebook community of more than 600, regularly traversing wheelchair-accessible trails around Portland. Members like Heidi Austin and Vanessa Rice cite the group as key in making outdoor adventures feasible, while Ouchida collaborates with local agencies to improve trail accessibility and safety for participants.

D.) RESIST! We Have Inherited a Legacy. Now It Is Our Turn. | Dr. Kirk Adams | August 24, 2026

Here, Dr. Kirk Adams invites readers to the free livestreamed launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, from 11:00 a.m. to noon Pacific (2:00 to 3:00 p.m. Eastern), and argues that the Coalition is inheriting a legacy rather than inventing one. Writing from a visit to Oakland in the Black Panther Party’s sixtieth anniversary year, he looks past the iconography to the Party’s Community Survival Programs, the free breakfasts, health clinics, sickle-cell testing, legal services and support for seniors and disabled people, and draws out the line that anchors the piece: resistance isn’t only about what we stand against, it is about what we build together.

E.) How Russia Is Using Disabled Soldiers for Frontline Assaults | Forbes.com | August 16, 2026

Wounded and disabled Russian soldiers, including men on crutches, are being returned to the front lines in Ukraine amid major manpower shortages, with reports citing them as decoys to draw Ukrainian drone fire. Mykola Melnyk, a former Ukrainian officer, and Russian sources describe a military system willing to sacrifice such troops for minor territorial gains. Analysts warn this attritional approach could signal how Moscow might respond in future conflicts with NATO.

August 31, 2026 📅️

2.) Access Information News Welcomes Jeremy Grandstaff and The Inspiration Foundation | Aaron Di Blasi, Publisher | August 31, 2026

Please join me in giving a warm welcome to Jeremy Grandstaff and The Inspiration Foundation, who has so very graciously agreed to support the ongoing distribution of Access Information News via sponsorship. If you enjoy reading Access Information News for free each week, it is Sponsors like Jeremy Grandstaff and The Inspiration Foundation that make it possible. And as I always say, these are the people, businesses and organizations that deserve your attention. Because they are the ones paying attention to the needs of the disability community.

The Inspiration Foundation is a 501(c)(3) public nonprofit working to increase the employment rate of people with disabilities. It was founded in 2006 by Isaac Shapiro and Mike Ghesser, the co-founders of the bath and body care brand Cleanlogic, and named for Isaac’s mother, Beatriz “Bea” Shapiro, who lost her sight to retinitis pigmentosa at about seven years old. Bea went on to become a long-distance runner, to found a technology training center for blind and visually impaired people, and to work as an assistive technology specialist for the State of Arizona. Her frustration was a practical one: the assistive technology disabled jobseekers were being trained on was too often out of date before they ever reached an interview. For its first two decades the Foundation answered that directly, awarding grants to nonprofit organizations serving blind and low-vision people so they could put current screen readers and Braille displays in front of the people who need them, including a dedicated fund for VisionServe Alliance member organizations.

In 2026 the Foundation appointed Jeremy Grandstaff as its first Executive Director. Grandstaff is blind, holds degrees in management information systems and organization development from Bowling Green State University, and brings two decades of organizational development and change management experience to the role. Under his leadership the Foundation has set a goal of increasing employment for people with disabilities by ten percent over the next five years, pursued through two pipelines running at once: a stronger pipeline of candidates, supported by the technology grant program, and a pipeline of employers who are actively hiring, promoting and retaining people with disabilities. The employer side of that work is being formalized into a certification called the Inspiration Seal, currently in pilot while its criteria are developed. Organizations interested in the technology grant program can reach Jeremy Grandstaff directly at jgrandstaff@inspirationfoundation.org 📧️.

3.) Tactile Revolution, An Exhibit Of Art Meant To Be Touched | Even Grounds | August 31, 2026

An exhibit at the Northern Kentucky University features tactile and 3D printed art, visitors are encouraged to touch all the displayed objects. The exhibit features pieces of art, buildings, maps, biology tools and braille publications to help blind and visually impaired people to better understand the visual world. If you are in the Cincinnati area, you can visit the exhibit until September 17th.

August 28, 2026 📅️

4.) Has Shane Gotten The New Gene Therapy? | Squirmy and Grubs | YouTube.com | August 28, 2026

Following months of developments, Shane Burcaw and Hannah Burcaw share an update on the potential new gene therapy for Shane’s disability. The pair explain what has been happening behind the scenes since first raising the possibility, offering a window into the uncertainty and momentum surrounding the process.

5.) What It’s Really Like Being A Disabled Supermodel | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | August 28, 2026

Sitting down with model, actress, and advocate Jillian Mercado, Molly Burke traces Mercado’s path from an immigrant household and an early misdiagnosis to a career that challenged fashion’s narrow ideas of who belongs. Their conversation covers the Diesel campaign that accelerated Mercado’s rise, her work with major brands, and the stakes of more authentic disability and Latina representation on screen and in media.

6.) The Differences in Lived Experiences – No Shocker and No Shaker | BarrierFreeCanada.org | August 28, 2026

Barrier Free Canada argues that disability lived experience is not interchangeable, even among people with the same impairment. Using inaccessible websites and apps as examples, it calls on organizations to distinguish between tasks completed independently and those made possible by partners, family members, or support workers.

7.) This Is Our Season: Join Us September 1st When We Launch, Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity & Inclusion | DrKirkAdams.com | August 28, 2026

Dr. Kirk Adams will launch the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion in a free LinkedIn event on September 1, 2026, from 11 a.m. to noon Pacific. The coalition aims to connect diversity, accessibility, and human-rights advocates with resources, peer-learning circles, expert guidance, and collective-action support.

8.) Federal Panel Adopts Overhauled Autism Plan | DisabilityScoop.com | August 28, 2026

The Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee approved a 330-page strategic plan that recommends raising annual federal autism investment to more than $747.4 million, from $390.4 million. The plan shifts away from its seven-question structure, adds regression research and a precision therapeutics initiative, and drew process concerns from disability groups.

9.) New Medicaid Rules Could Impact Scores of Beneficiaries. Many May Not Know It | DisabilityScoop.com | August 28, 2026

Oregon is racing to notify roughly 600,000 Oregon Health Plan members who could face federal Medicaid work, school or volunteer requirements of at least 80 hours a month beginning next year. The Oregon Health Authority estimates up to 200,000 could lose coverage, as beneficiaries may not realize OHP and managed-care brands are Medicaid or know whether exemptions apply.

August 27, 2026 📅️

10.) The Cooking Without Looking TV Show Blind Visionaries Edition | Cooking Without Looking | YouTube.com | August 27, 2026

Sitting down with guest Allison Arbuckle, Sylvia Stinson-Perez spotlights the Blind Visionaries community and the practical conversations shaping accessible cooking. Michelle Ditter prepares cheeseburger mac and cheese before the panel turns to kitchen techniques, questions, and everyday considerations for blind, visually impaired, and low-vision cooks.

11.) The Willits Slide: Accessibility Advocates Mark Ten Years of Progress Mired With Problems | StreetsBlog.org | August 27, 2026

Ten years after Los Angeles committed nearly $1.4 billion over 30 years under the Willits Settlement, disability advocates staged The Willits Slide to protest uneven sidewalk-accessibility work. Settlement attorney Paula Pearlman praised curb-ramp gains but rated the city’s overall progress a three out of 10.

12.) Designing Digital Public Services That Work for Everyone | OpenAccessGovernment.org | August 27, 2026

Digital exclusion in UK public services now stems as much from service design, support and user confidence as from connectivity, according to Elizabeth Anderson of the Digital Poverty Alliance and Cognizant’s Yatin Mahandru. They call for mobile-aware design, inclusive testing, better measures of abandonment and support demand, plus telephone, face-to-face and paper alternatives.

13.) Govt Invites Disability Advocates to Test Accessibility Features Ahead of New Huanggang Port Opening | TheStandard.com.hk | August 27, 2026

Hong Kong’s Security Bureau invited disability advocates and social service groups to test barrier-free facilities at the new Huanggang Port before it enters service. The on-site trial covered tactile paving, accessible toilets, lifts and dedicated clearance channels, with immigration, customs, transport and design agencies gathering suggestions for operational refinements.

14.) Guardians Are Supposed to Care for Our Most Vulnerable. Why Are Exploitation Cases Skyrocketing? | DisabilityScoop.com | August 27, 2026

New Jersey’s Guardianship Monitoring Program reported 694 escalated concerns to judges in 2025, up from 252 in 2024, including nearly 90 cases involving inappropriate, un-itemized or unexplained disbursements. The state has more than 37,000 guardianships overseeing $1.2 billion in reported assets.

15.) Meta Smart Glasses and AI Drones Open Warehouse Jobs to Blind Workers | BigGo.com | August 27, 2026

Bosma Enterprises is using Meta smart glasses, Gather AI inventory drones and iPad screen readers to enable blind workers to handle warehouse tasks. Gather AI drones can finish counts in minutes rather than days, as transportation, warehousing and utilities reported 392,000 open jobs in June, up 87,000 year over year.

16.) Federal Appeals Court Sides With Lyft in Wheelchair Accessibility Lawsuit | WestchesterNews12.com | August 27, 2026

A federal appeals court ruled Lyft is not required to provide wheelchair-accessible vehicles nationwide, affirming a lower-court win for the ride-hailing company. Westchester Disabled on the Move alleged limits on vehicles for fixed-frame wheelchairs violated the Americans with Disabilities Act and New York Human Rights Law; the court found its proposed remedies would not deliver effective accessible transportation.

August 26, 2026 📅️

17.) I’m Not The Dad I Thought I’d Be… | Legally Blind No Limits | YouTube.com | August 26, 2026

Navigating a hectic school drop-off, Legally Blind No Limits recounts the first day at a new school with his seven-year-old son as a legally blind parent. With his white cane and mobility training guiding the route, the experience becomes an unexpected reflection on his son’s growing instinct to help lead the way.

18.) Inclusive Arts Gallery – Enrico Bisenzi (A11ytalks – August 2026) | Accessibility Talks | YouTube.com | August 26, 2026

Showcasing Inclusive Arts Gallery, Enrico Bisenzi traces artists and ideas that have expanded artistic expression and social participation for people with disabilities. The project organizes its profiles in reverse chronological order, drawing on encounters from Bisenzi’s three decades in higher education across art, music, and dance.

19.) Council Weighs Options to Address $74 Million Accessibility Backlog | CivicLex.org | August 26, 2026

Lexington Council reviewed a WT Group AEC plan to remedy roughly 19,430 accessibility barriers at 188 parks and city facilities, with phased fixes estimated at more than $74 million over 20 years. Finance Commissioner Erin Hensley said asset replacements could be bonded or supported by the Parks Fund, while repairs must fit the operating budget; Council allocated $1.5 million for FY2027.

20.) How Dolly Parton Helped the World – From Children’s Books to Supporting Covid Vaccine | BBC.com | August 26, 2026

Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library has distributed more than 332.4 million free books to children in the US, Canada, UK, Ireland and Australia since 1995. Her philanthropy also included a $1m gift that helped fund an early Moderna Covid-19 vaccine trial, disaster relief in Tennessee, and tuition for Dollywood employees.

21.) Rainbow Crosswalks Could Cause Optical Illusions, City Committee Warns | SooToday.com | August 26, 2026

Sault Ste. Marie’s accessibility advisory committee says painted pedestrian routes, including rainbow crosswalks, can create optical illusions that confuse or disorient people with vision loss. Council allocated $25,000 on Aug. 10 for a permanent 2SLGBTQIA+ public-art mural instead.

22.) Existing Blood Tests May Help Identify Future Disability Risk | TechnologyNetworks.com | August 26, 2026

A Keio University-led study found that elevated beta-2-microglobulin and cystatin C predicted future disability among 230 disability-free Japanese adults aged 85-89, followed for about 4.5 years. The associations, with hazard ratios of 1.35 and 1.42, respectively, were replicated in Italy’s InCHIANTI cohort, linking kidney function and chronic inflammation to loss of independence.

23.) Lyft Removes Barrier for Riders With Developmental Disabilities | DisabilityScoop.com | August 26, 2026

Lyft updated Lyft Pass for Public Funding so Medicaid home and community-based services recipients can create accounts and request prepaid rides without a personal payment card or pre-authorization check. Betty Yen, Lyft’s director of healthcare partnerships, said 15% to 20% of LPPF participants are unbanked.

24.) Dizon Calls DPWH Compliance With Accessibility Law “Terrible” | NewsInfo.inquirer.net | August 26, 2026

Public Works and Highways Secretary Vince Dizon called the department’s compliance with the Philippines’ Accessibility Law “terrible” during a House briefing on its proposed 2027 budget. DPWH says its allocation for PWD, senior-citizen, and gender-responsive infrastructure rose from P117 million to P510 million, though Dizon and lawmakers said it remains insufficient.

August 25, 2026 📅️

25.) I Blindfolded My Fiancé For 24 Hours | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | August 25, 2026

For a 24-hour empathy experiment, Molly Burke blindfolds her fiance and documents how he navigates a day without sight. The challenge puts everyday routines at the center of a conversation about accessibility, independence, and the assumptions sighted people can bring to daily life.

26.) Lexington Needs to Spend $74M Over 20 Years to Make Public Spaces Accessible | Kentucky.com | August 25, 2026

Lexington’s new ADA Transition Plan puts the cost of bringing parks, government buildings and other public spaces into compliance at $74.45 million over 20 years. WT Group AEC assessed more than 4,500 acres and recommends a $21.9 million first phase; the city has set aside $1.5 million while officials weigh taxes, bonds and grants.

27.) Daughter’s Cancer Treatment Led Milwaukee Mom to Champion First City-Owned Universally Accessible Playground | WPR.org | August 25, 2026

After her daughter Stella’s brain-tumor treatment left her needing to relearn basic abilities, Rese Schneider organized a $2 million push for Stella’s Playground at Milwaukee’s Kilbourne Reservoir Park. The city-backed design includes wheelchair-friendly surfaces, sensory spaces and an adaptive sports court; more than $1 million has been raised toward a planned May 7, 2027 opening.

28.) AI Weeds Out Job Applicants With Disabilities, Lawsuit Claims | DisabilityScoop.com | August 25, 2026

Workday faces a federal lawsuit alleging its AI hiring tools automatically screen out older, minority and disabled applicants. Judge Rita F. Lin dismissed intentional-discrimination claims but allowed disparate-impact allegations to proceed, while Workday says its tools assess qualifications rather than protected traits and retain human oversight.

29.) States See Spike in Special Ed Complaints | DisabilityScoop.com | August 25, 2026

Written special education complaints rose nearly 48% across 33 reporting states, reaching 12,398 in the 2025-2026 school year after remaining below 8,400 in each of the prior two years. Chad Rummel, CEO of the Council for Exceptional Children, said delays and widespread dismissals at the Education Department’s OCR may be eroding families’ confidence in federal recourse.

30.) They’re More Than Group Homes. For the Residents Who Live There, It’s Just Home | DisabilityScoop.com | August 25, 2026

The Arc Erie County New York runs 25 Individualized Residential Alternative homes serving 177 people, from medically staffed group homes to lower-oversight apartments. CEO Douglas DiGesare says they can be permanent homes or a bridge to independent living; demand has left 1,364 people on the waiting list.

31.) Braille Is Beautiful, and Braille Is Literacy | DrKirkAdams.com | August 25, 2026

Aaron Di Blasi argues that braille remains a core literacy medium, distinct from speech output, while challenging the often-repeated claim that only 10% of blind people read braille. He points to the 2026-2027 ICEVI and World Blind Union global survey, workplace research, refreshable displays, and youth programs including NFB BELL Academy and the Braille Challenge.

32.) Remarkable World Commentary Episode #108: Interview With Peggy Chong, the Blind History Lady | DonnaJodhan.com | August 25, 2026

Peggy Chong, known as The Blind History Lady, traces overlooked accounts of blind Americans in Donna J. Jodhan’s Episode #108 podcast. Chong recounts researching Minnesota congressman and senator Thomas David Schall, a Colorado cigar merchant’s 1909 railroad case, and adaptive work methods while arguing that persistence, rather than money or schooling, shapes success.

August 24, 2026 📅️

33.) Disney Is Setting The Standard For Accessibility At D23 | Driven by Purpose | YouTube.com | August 24, 2026

Sitting down to discuss Disney’s approach at D23, Isaac, Evan, and Mike examine how the convention made participation more practical and welcoming for attendees with disabilities. The conversation weighs measures including wheelchair access and ASL interpretation against the broader business case for embedding inclusion into culture, while considering safety for power wheelchair users in dense crowds.

34.) After Years of Federal Oversight, Georgia’s Disability Care System Faces a New Test | GeorgiaRecorder.com | August 24, 2026

DOJ’s June memo says federal disability law does not require states to provide certain community-based services or authorize federal monitoring, raising fears over enforcement of Georgia’s Olmstead settlement. Commissioner Kevin Tanner says the state will comply, though 7,200 Georgians remain on the NOW/COMP waiver planning list.

35.) Trump Puts Autistic Kids in the Spotlight and Cuts Agencies Built to Protect Them | CBSNews.com | August 24, 2026

To this end, BFC/CSB is seeking endorsements from national disability organizations to build a non-partisan community coalition. BFC/CSB would also like to identify point persons from these organizations to act as key contacts.

The steering committee of BFC/CSB has drafted a set of principles concerning a CDA that are drawn from the principles that underpin the provincial disability legislation in Ontario and Manitoba. About: The Inspiration Foundation is a 501(c)(3) public nonprofit working to increase the employment rate of people with disabilities. It was founded in 2006 by Isaac Shapiro and Mike Ghesser, the co-founders of the bath and body care brand Cleanlogic, and named for Isaac’s mother, Beatriz “Bea” Shapiro, who lost her sight to retinitis pigmentosa at about seven years old. Bea went on to become a long-distance runner, to found a technology training center for blind and visually impaired people, and to work as a vocational rehabilitation counselor for the State of Arizona. Her frustration was a practical one: the assistive technology disabled jobseekers were being trained on was too often out of date before they ever reached an interview. For its first two decades the Foundation answered that directly, awarding grants to nonprofit organizations serving blind and low-vision people so they could put current screen readers and Braille displays in front of the people who need them, including a dedicated fund for VisionServe Alliance member organizations.

In 2026 the Foundation appointed Jeremy Grandstaff as its first Executive Director. Grandstaff is blind, holds degrees in management information systems and organization development from Bowling Green State University, and brings two decades of organizational development and change management experience to the role. Under his leadership the Foundation has set a goal of increasing employment for people with disabilities by ten percent over the next five years, pursued through two pipelines running at once: a stronger pipeline of candidates, supported by the technology grant program, and a pipeline of employers who are actively hiring, promoting and retaining people with disabilities. The employer side of that work is being formalized into a certification called the Inspiration Seal, currently in pilot while its criteria are developed. Organizations interested in the technology grant program can reach Jeremy Grandstaff directly at jgrandstaff@inspirationfoundation.org.

item.title: It Started With Braille on a Bath Sponge: Welcome, Jeremy Grandstaff and The Inspiration Foundation
item.dc:creator: Access Information News
item.description:
Here, Aaron Di Blasi, Publisher for the Access Information News weekly newsletter, welcomes Jeremy Grandstaff and The Inspiration Foundation as the publication's newest sponsor, and traces the unlikely path that brought them there. It begins on a supermarket shelf, with the working Braille printed on Cleanlogic's bath and body packaging, a feature that required moving an entire product line off plastic and onto paper, and one that exists because of Beatriz "Bea" Shapiro, who lost her sight to retinitis pigmentosa at about age seven and spent her career training blind people to use adaptive technology and placing them into jobs. Her son Isaac Shapiro and his business partner Mike Ghesser built Cleanlogic around that idea in 2006, and run an American production floor in Audubon, Pennsylvania staffed substantially by people with disabilities under a program they call Purchase To Employ. Di Blasi is careful to separate what is independently documented, the Overbrook School for the Blind hires, the twenty-nine jobs brought back from overseas, the reported wages and benefits, the NBC News coverage, and Pennsylvania's 2025 Governor's Achievement Award, from the share-of-workforce percentages the company reports about itself.

The post It Started With Braille on a Bath Sponge: Welcome, Jeremy Grandstaff and The Inspiration Foundation appeared first on Access Information News.
item.content:encoded:
Our newest sponsor is a twenty-year-old nonprofit that has just hired its first executive director, and the story of how it got here runs through a supermarket shelf, a production floor in Pennsylvania, and a woman who lost her sight at seven years old.

Reach onto a supermarket shelf for a bath sponge and you’re using your eyes to tell one package from another. The color. The picture. The size of the type. If you can’t see, then you’re relying on somebody else, or on a guess.

Unless the package has Braille on it. Not a logo. Not a gesture in the direction of accessibility. Working Braille, printed on the box, that tells you what you are holding.

Getting here meant moving an entire product line off plastic packaging and onto paper, because plastic couldn’t carry the Braille. That decision traces back to a woman who lost her sight at about seven years old. It is also, by a route worth explaining, the reason this newsletter has a new sponsor this week.

Please join me in welcoming Jeremy Grandstaff and The Inspiration Foundation.

The Woman It Started With

Her name is Beatriz Shapiro. Bea.

Retinitis pigmentosa took her sight at around age seven. It did not take anything else. She became a long-distance runner. She founded a technology training centre for blind and visually impaired people. She works as an assistive technology specialist for the State of Arizona, which is to say she has spent her working life on the precise problem this article is about: getting disabled people into work.

Her son is Isaac Shapiro. In 2006 he and his business partner Mike Ghesser founded a bath and body care brand called Cleanlogic, and they put Braille on it.

Translation: the accessibility feature was not added to the product later. The product was built around it.

A Company That Hires the People It Serves

Cleanlogic makes exfoliating cloths, sponges, buffers and scrubbers, at everyday prices, and sells them through Walmart, Target, CVS, Meijer, Nordstrom, ShopRite, H-E-B, Sprouts, Ulta and Amazon. Ordinary products in an ordinary aisle.

The part that matters is not on the shelf. It is in Audubon, Pennsylvania, where the company runs an American production floor staffed substantially by people with disabilities.

Mike Ghesser’s eldest daughter, Rosie, has intellectual and physical disabilities. Together, he and the rest of the team built the hiring model, and gave it a name that removes any doubt about how it is funded: Purchase To Employ. You buy the sponge. The company employs somebody.

Now the numbers, and I want to be careful about which are which. In 2021 Cleanlogic moved work away from factories in China and back to Pennsylvania, hired seven people from the Overbrook School for the Blind, and packed its entire 2021 holiday gift-set run with blind and low-vision team members. In October 2024 it opened an expanded facility and brought twenty-nine jobs back from overseas. Chain Drug Review, which toured the operation, reported wages of seventeen to twenty dollars an hour with health insurance and access to a 401(k). NBC News filmed on site. The Eagles Autism Foundation took part in the opening. On April 30, 2025, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania presented the company with its Governor’s Achievement Award for Employer of Workers with Disabilities, alongside the state Office of Vocational Rehabilitation.

Twenty Years on, a First Executive Director

Alongside the company, Isaac and Mike started The Inspiration Foundation, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit named for Bea and built around a specific frustration of hers: that the technology disabled people were being trained on was so often out of date. For most of its twenty years the Foundation did one thing, quietly and well. Small grants, up to around two thousand dollars, to non-profit organizations serving blind and low-vision people, so they could buy current screen readers and Braille displays.

This year it decided to grow, and for the first time in its history it hired an executive director.

Jeremy Grandstaff is blind. He attended a school for blind children through fifth grade and was arguing for accessible books and Braille literacy long before he was old enough to vote. He holds two degrees from Bowling Green State University, a bachelor’s in management information systems and a master’s in organization development, and he has spent roughly two decades in organizational development and change management.

By twenty-six he was running a team of about fifty-five at IBM Global Services. He spent nearly twenty years as a principal of his own consultancy. He was Member Services Director at the Alliance for Biking & Walking, a coalition then representing more than two hundred advocacy organizations, and, a detail I enjoyed, being where I am, he wrote the strategic plan for Bike Cleveland. He gave a TEDx talk at TEDxYpsilanti on June 27, 2025, called “A Blind Man’s Path to Opportunity.” He works with a seeing eye dog named Ozzy.

In his first six months he reports having increased the Foundation’s grantmaking by roughly twelve thousand dollars across ten grants.

Two Pipelines, and a Deadline

Here is what he is actually trying to do, in his own framing.

The goal is to increase employment for people with disabilities by ten percent over the next five years. He calls it aggressive. And he’s right.

He’s building it out of two pipelines. The first is a stronger pipeline of candidates, and that is what the technology grants are for, making sure disabled jobseekers are trained on equipment that is current, rather than on whatever was donated a decade ago. The second is a pipeline of employers who are actively hiring, promoting and retaining disabled staff.

Read those three verbs again. Not “open to.” Not “willing to consider.” Hiring, promoting, retaining. The third one is where a great many corporate disability initiatives quietly come apart, and it is telling that it is written into the goal rather than left as an afterthought.

The employer half of that work is being formalised into a certification called the Inspiration Seal, which is at present a pilot with its criteria still being written.

Translation: the Foundation spent twenty years improving the supply of well-prepared candidates, and has now concluded that improving the supply alone was never going to be enough.

How This Happened

I will say plainly how these introductions came about, because they came from the same person both times.

Dr. Kirk Adams introduced me to Jeremy in October 2024, having seen the two of us circling the same work. Nearly a year later, in September 2025, he reconnected me with Isaac. Kirk sponsors this newsletter himself and sits on the editorial team at our sister publication, Top Tech Tidbits. He has honed carefully the incredible superpower of knowing which two people in this field ought to be talking to each other.

Regular readers will also already know the Driven By Purpose Podcast, which has sponsored Access Information News since November 3, 2025. It is co-hosted by Isaac Shapiro, by Mike Ghesser, and by Evan Rosenblum, a Daytime Emmy-nominated journalist who spent about two decades building TMZ and TMZ Sports. Rosenblum’s daughter Sydney was born at twenty-five weeks and lives with severe cerebral palsy; he founded the Sydney Strong Run Club, whose members run 5k and 10k races alongside participants using running chairs.

So this week’s new sponsor does not arrive out of nowhere. They arrive from a group of people several of you already read every week.

What a Sponsorship Actually Buys, in Both Directions

For those who want to know what sponsorship does here: it keeps this newsletter free to read for more than 47,000 blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled readers every Monday morning, along with the caregivers, companies and organizations that serve and support them. Access Information News is operated as a not-for-profit project. Funds go to distribution, and when sponsor slots do not fill, my company, Mind Vault Solutions, covers the difference.

It also opens a door the other way. Sponsors join the PWD Media Distribution Co-op, a network in which people and organizations with verified blind, low vision and disability audiences share their distribution channels with one another. As of this writing that is thirty members across forty-six connected channels, reaching 199,512 disability-specific readers with every post.

Which is the honest description of what happened here. In his words and mine, we maximize each other’s reach. The mission statement of the PWD Media Co-op reads: “Amplifying disability voices through collective reach.”

One more thing, since it is the question I am asked most often by readers and least often by advertisers. Yes I vet everybody, and no, I do not accept everybody. Just ask around. I will not write an article about any person, product, service, company or organization (potential sponsor or not) that I have not vetted first. And if that check does not come back clean, I decline the money. A welcome in this newsletter is designed to carry weight.

In His Own Words

“I’m really excited to lead the Inspiration Foundation to sponsor Access Information News. Not only is it a great publication putting out fantastic ideas and actionable things that people can mimic within their own organizations, it’s an opportunity to connect and share, not just what we’re doing, but what other people can learn from us, and what we can learn from them.”

— Jeremy Grandstaff, Executive Director, The Inspiration Foundation

Welcome aboard, Jeremy. Thank you so much for joining us.

Where to Find Them

  • The Inspiration Foundation: https://inspirationfoundation.org/
  • Technology Grant Program: Jeremy Grandstaff, jgrandstaff@inspirationfoundation.org 📧️
  • Cleanlogic: https://cleanlogic.com/
  • The Driven By Purpose Podcast: https://thedrivenbypurposepodcast.com/
  • The PWD Media Distribution Co-op: https://at-newswire.com/pwd-mdc/

” The greatest barrier to accessibility is indifference. “

Aaron Di Blasi, PMP
Engineer, Educator, Advocate, Publisher & Journalist

item.title: Welcome, National Organization on Disability: A Sponsor Worth Forwarding to Your Employer
item.dc:creator: Aaron Di Blasi
item.description:
Here, Aaron Di Blasi, Publisher for the Access Information News weekly newsletter, welcomes the National Organization on Disability as the publication's newest Sponsor, effective Monday, September 7, 2026, and argues that this one is a genuinely different kind of Sponsor. Nearly every Sponsor comes to reach the newsletter's blind, low vision, deaf, deafblind, neurodivergent and disabled readership directly. NOD does not. Founded in 1982 by Alan A. Reich out of the United Nations International Year of Disabled Persons, and led since May 2024 by President and CEO Beth Sirull, the Washington, DC nonprofit sells to corporate human resources departments and works what Sirull calls the demand side of disability employment, changing how companies hire, onboard, accommodate and promote disabled workers. Rather than paper over that distinction, Di Blasi names it plainly: there are hundreds of organizations working on making you ready for the job, and very few working on making the job ready for you.

The post Welcome, National Organization on Disability: A Sponsor Worth Forwarding to Your Employer appeared first on Access Information News.
item.content:encoded:
Our newest Sponsor does not sell anything to you. It sells to the people who decide whether you get hired, and that is exactly why I wanted them here.

If you are blind, low vision, deaf, deafblind, neurodivergent or disabled and you have ever worked, you already know the part of the job search that no amount of preparation fixes.

You can master your screen reader. You can hold the degree, the certification, the fifteen years experience. You can write the cover letter, rehearse the answers, arrive early and perform well. And you can still lose the role to something that happened on the other side of the desk entirely, in a conversation you were never in, conducted by a hiring manager who had never worked with anyone like you and quietly decided it would be complicated.

That’s not a skills problem. It has never been a skills problem. It’s a demand-side problem, and it is not one you can solve from your own desk no matter how good you are.

Welcome, National Organization on Disability

NOD is our newest Sponsor here at Access Information News, effective Monday, September 7, 2026. And they are a genuinely different kind of Sponsor for this newsletter, because almost everything they do happens on the employer’s side of that desk.

Most organizations in this space work on preparing disabled people for employers. National Organization on Disability works on preparing employers for disabled people. They are one of the very few doing it from that direction, and it is the direction the problem actually lives in.

What NOD Is, Plainly

National Organization on Disability is a Washington, DC nonprofit that has been working on disability employment since 1982. It came out of the United Nations International Year of Disabled Persons, and was founded by Alan A. Reich, the first person ever to address the UN General Assembly from a wheelchair.

A note on identity, because plenty of otherwise careful sources get it wrong. NOD is not the National Council on Disability, the independent federal agency at ncd.gov. Nearly identical names, completely different organizations. NOD is a private nonprofit that employers pay.

Today NOD’s work runs on four legs: a paid corporate membership network called the Leadership Council, a confidential benchmarking assessment attached to a public recognition, a paid on-demand training platform, and federal policy advocacy backed by university research partners.

It is led by Beth Sirull, President and Chief Executive Officer since May 2024, who came to disability employment from impact investing and philanthropic management rather than from the disability rights movement. Alongside her are Charles-Edouard Catherine, Vice President of Corporate and Government Relations and a Paralympian, and Sara Walsh, Chief Operations and Finance Officer.

Why This Sponsor Is Different

I want to be straight with you, because you will notice it yourself within a minute of visiting their website.

Nearly every Sponsor in this newsletter is here because they want to reach you. They make a screen reader, an app, a service, a piece of hardware, and you are the customer. NOD is not built that way. Their paying customers are corporate human resources departments. Their product is a change in how a company hires, onboards, trains, accommodates, promotes and retains disabled workers.

Beth Sirull describes it as working the demand side of the disability employment problem, as distinct from the very large supply side made up of organizations that prepare disabled people for work.

Translation: there are hundreds of organizations working on making you ready for the job. There are very few working on making the job ready for you. NOD is one of them.

What You Can Actually Use Yourself

The picture is not quite as one-sided as it first looks. Several things at NOD an individual reader can reach directly, without going through an employer at all.

  • EnAble Learning, individual licence. Their on-demand course platform is $100 per year for an individual, discounted to $50 for a first year as an early adopter.
  • Network of Allies. NOD’s individual membership, as distinct from the corporate Leadership Council.
  • Virtual career fairs. Real hiring events with real employers, free for jobseekers. The next one runs September 10, 2026 and lists Sedgwick, the American Heart Association and CoBank among the participants.
  • CEO Office Hours. Open Zoom sessions with Beth Sirull, no ticket price listed. One ran on May 6, 2026 on inclusive talent acquisition, and the next is set for December 17, 2026.
  • Technology and the Disability Experience. Their annual showcase, this year on Wednesday, October 1, 2026 at the Times Center in New York. Standard tickets are $199. Last year drew 250-plus people and featured Aira, Be My Eyes, the Howe Innovation Center at Perkins School for the Blind, Inclusively, Target and Toyota.
  • The Speakers Bureau. Launched March 24, 2026, roughly 29 speakers including Lex Gillette, Tiffany Yu, Keely Cat-Wells, Catarina Rivera and Josh Basile. Booking is normally an employer’s purchase, but worth knowing if your workplace asks.

EnAble Learning

When I asked Beth what NOD is pushing hardest right now, EnAble Learning was the first thing she named.

It went live in 2026, and it is a straightforward idea executed well: modular, self-paced, roughly hour-long courses that teach a workforce how disability inclusion actually works in practice. The current catalogue includes Disability 101, Managing Teams in the Age of Rising Mental Health Challenges, AI, Emerging Technology, and Accessibility, and Neurodiversity at Work. There is also a Microsoft Accessibility Fundamentals course offered in collaboration with Microsoft.

For employers it scales down to $50 per learner per year up to 250 learners, $25 per learner per year from 251 to 2,500, and negotiated access above that including export into a company’s own learning system.

Translation: if your employer has ever said that disability training was too expensive or too hard to source, that excuse now costs them twenty-five dollars a head.

The Rule Change Landing on September 21, 2026

This is the part I would forward to your employer today rather than next month, as I believe it is the reason NOD’s timing here is most fortuitous.

On August 21, 2026, a final rule was published in the Federal Register, document 2026-17115 at 91 FR 54482. It takes effect on September 21, 2026. It rescinds the Section 503 requirement that federal contractors set a 7 percent disability utilization goal, and it removes the requirement that they invite applicants and employees to identify themselves as disabled. The veterans equivalent under VEVRAA is untouched.

For roughly a decade, that 7 percent goal and that self-identification invitation are what made a great many large employers pay attention to disability hiring at all. They were the compliance stick. As of September 21, 2026 for federal contractors, the stick is gone.

What is left is the business case, and the business case now has to do the entire job on its own.

I want to be careful here about who is saying what. NOD is not named anywhere in that rule. That paragraph is my analysis as a publisher, not their position. But it is difficult to look at an organization whose entire model is persuading employers to do this voluntarily, and at a rule that removes the requirement to do it involuntarily, and not conclude that their work matters considerably more on September 22 than it did on September 20.

What NOD Sells Employers

This section is for the readers among you who hire, who manage, who sit in HR, or who are close enough to someone who does that you could forward this to them.

The Leadership Council is NOD’s paid employer membership, currently 35 member organizations, structured in four tiers including two sized for mid-market companies: Medium Enterprise at 251 to 2,000 employees and Small Organization up to 250. Named members include Boeing, Eli Lilly, EY, Hilton, Kaiser Permanente, KPMG, Marriott, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley, PwC, Target, Toyota and Wells Fargo. Membership buys disability inclusion specialists, peer networking, talent acquisition support, learning seats and event tickets. At the Premium tier it also buys either two secured entry-level hires or ten qualified candidate referrals through their partner James Emmett & Company.

The Disability Inclusion Blueprint is their free confidential self-assessment, benchmarking a company across talent outcomes, strategy and policies, and practices and programs. Top-quartile participants who opt in earn the Leading Disability Employer Seal, which has no tiers.

One honest caveat, and I would rather you hear it from me. The Blueprint survey is not running in 2026. NOD states it plainly on their own site, and they expect to move to an every-other-year cadence beginning in 2027. If you go looking for it this year you will not find it, so plan around that.

Through their Employer Disability Practices Center, NOD tracked 257 companies that completed their assessment at least twice between 2021 and 2024, and reports that those with fully integrated disability inclusion hired twice as many people with disabilities and promoted five times as many. Those are NOD’s own findings rather than independently replicated results, and I am flagging them as such.

How This Happened

This one did not arrive the way most of them do.

It began on April 10, 2026, with an introductory meeting with Aaron Brown, NOD’s Director of Resource Development. That same day I made an introduction of my own, connecting Aaron Brown with Dr. Kirk Adams.

Over the following months Dr. Adams did what he does best, which is build relationships. Second only to his ability to make connections. He met with Aaron Brown shortly after my introduction and has been in conversation with Beth Sirull directly, whom he will be interviewing for his podcast. When NOD and I finally sat down together, we already shared common ground, and it was Dr. Adams that helped to build that synergy. His guidance has taught me that having a solution is not enough. You have to locate and connect with the people that need that solution, and then explain to them why they need it. Something he does exceptionally well. And as a result, something that I too have begun to do as well. Everyone talks the talk. Few walk the walk. Dr. Adams is one of those few.

For readers who do not know him: Dr. Kirk Adams is the former President and CEO of the American Foundation for the Blind and of The Lighthouse for the Blind in Seattle, Executive Director of the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion, Managing Director of Innovative Impact, LLC, and author of The Disability Dividend. He holds a PhD in Leadership and Change from Antioch University, where his dissertation studied blind adults successfully employed in American corporations. In the interest of full disclosure: Dr. Adams sponsors this newsletter himself, and he sits on the editorial team at our sister publication, Top Tech Tidbits.

On Thursday, August 27, 2026, I met Beth Sirull and Amber Cecil, NOD’s Director of Marketing and Communications, by video call. It was the first time any of us had met. I presented the full program, they asked a great many questions, and we found a considerable amount of common ground rather quickly. By the end of the call NOD had agreed to support the ongoing distribution of Access Information News.

Amber has been at NOD since April 2012, the longest-serving member of their senior staff. If NOD’s public voice has shifted over the last decade from awareness language to something written for a boardroom, that is largely her work.

What I Checked

Since it is the question I am asked most often by readers and least often by advertisers: yes, I vet everybody, and no, I do not accept everybody.

NOD’s finances, governance and filings are public and I read them. The one thing worth flagging is the one above that affects what you can do this year: the Blueprint survey is paused for 2026. Everything else is the ordinary texture of a forty-four-year-old nonprofit in a difficult funding climate, and none of it changed my view that this is serious work our readers benefit from.

Sponsors provide much-needed support in exchange for verified, measurable reach. They cannot buy our editorial judgement. This article was written from an objective point of view.

Where to Learn More

  • Website: https://nod.org/
  • EnAble Learning: https://enable.nod.org/
  • Address: 700 12th Street N.W., Suite 700, Washington, DC 20005

What to Do With This

You have just read a great deal about an organization that does not sell to you. So let’s close with what each of you can actually do.

  • If you are job seeking: put the September virtual career fair in your calendar, and look at who is participating before you decide whether it is worth your time.
  • If you are employed: forward this article to whoever owns hiring or learning and development at your organization. That single act is the entire mechanism by which this Sponsorship pays you back. EnAble Learning costs your employer twenty-five dollars a head.
  • If you hire, manage, or work in HR: the Leadership Council has tiers built for companies with fewer than 250 employees, so this is not only a Fortune 500 conversation. And the September 21, 2026 rule change is worth an hour of your attention this month regardless of what you decide about NOD.
  • If you are a caregiver, family member or advocate: the person you support is going to encounter an employer eventually. Knowing that an organization exists whose entire job is working on that employer is worth carrying with you.

A Note of Thanks

Access Information News is operated as a not-for-profit project by Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. All Sponsorship dollars are held in escrow and used solely to fund the ongoing distribution of the publication. When the Sponsor cap is not met, Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. covers the difference.

If you enjoy reading Access Information News for free each and every week, it is Sponsors like National Organization on Disability that make it possible. Without their support, there would be no Access Information News.

Every Sponsor of this publication also joins the PWD Media Distribution Co-op, which stands at 30 members across 46 connected channels, reaching 199,512 disability-specific readers with every post, as of this writing.

Beth and Amber, thank you both for the conversation, for the questions, and for saying yes. Dr. Adams, thank you for the months of quiet work between the introduction and the handshake.

Welcome, National Organization on Disability. So very happy to have you with us.

Cheers,

” The greatest barrier to accessibility is indifference. “

Aaron Di Blasi, PMP
Engineer, Educator, Advocate, Publisher & Journalist
President & Sr. PMP, Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd., PR Director: AT-Newswire, Publisher: AI-Weekly, Top Tech Tidbits, Access Information News, Title II Today

♿️ The Week’s News in Access Information

Access Information News. The world’s #1 online resource for current news and trends in access information.

A Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. Publication

Subscribers:  47,058 🔢️ opt-in subscribers were sent this issue via email.

Social Media:  195,488 🔢️ readers were sent this issue via social media, courtesy of the PWD Media Distribution Co-Op.

Share: Facebook | X (Twitter) | LinkedIn | Email | Web Link | How to read this newsletter if you are blind or low-vision.

Section Jumper: Sponsors | Access Awareness | Featured Advertisement | News | Featured Events | Classified Ads | Supporters | News Team | Subscription Information

Sponsors 🏅️

Access Awareness: Updates That Matter ♿️

He Blindfolded His Sister For A Day To Show Her What His Life Is Like… | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | August 18, 2026

Showcasing a personal experiment, Molly Burke invites viewers to witness her sister navigating daily life blindfolded, offering direct insight into the realities of living with vision loss. The episode underscores everyday challenges and moments of empathy, highlighting Burke’s ongoing commitment to disability inclusion and awareness.

This Week’s Featured Advertisement ️

Sponsorship Packages Currently Available: Join Industry Leaders in Supporting Free Access Information News For Disabled Readers All Over The World While Increasing Traffic To Your Properties Each Week. Advertise in every issue. Or just one.

Join Access Information News as a Sponsor today and begin reaching over 45,000 access information readers each week, all while supporting the ongoing distribution of Access Information News for those very same readers. Only $200 / month.

Key Newsletter Statistics:

  • Subscribers: 45,000 + per week and growing.
  • Open Rate: 47% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Click Rate: 34% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Bounce Rate: 1.2% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Ad CTRs: 2-12% (Average. Last 12 months.)

Benefits All Sponsors Receive:

  • One (1) Sponsor Profile on the Access Information News website, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Profile in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement on the Access Information News home page + every page of the website (Right Side Bar: Sponsors), for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Classified Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Membership in the PWD Media Co-Op, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • 50% Discount on all Sponsored News Article Advertisements, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Free link tracking, for all time.
  • Permanent SEO benefits. (All Sponsor Profiles are archived on the Access Information News website at the close of Sponsorship. Driving traffic back to your properties for all time.
  • Gratitude from over 45,000 blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled professionals, educators, and enthusiasts, all over the world, along with the caregivers, companies and organizations that serve and support them, for keeping Access Information News free to read each week.

With additional benefits for Sponsors who choose to pay quarterly or annually. Learn more about Sponsorship today. today.

News 📰️

👉 Submit a news article for free here, with timing and placement determined by our editors.

👉 Submit a Sponsored News Article here, with timing and placement determined by you.

1.) Top 5 Most Clicked News Articles From Last Week 📊️

A.) Recruiting College Talent With Disabilities: What Works, What Doesn’t, And Why | National Organization on Disability | YouTube.com | August 13, 2026

In this analytical framing, National Organization on Disability closely examines the persistent hurdles recruiters face when engaging college students with disabilities. Supported by recent NOD research, the session highlights concrete steps for improving campus connections and creating accessible environments where early-career professionals can succeed.

B.) Podcast: Remarkable World Commentary Episode #102: Interview with Aaron Di Blasi, Sr. PMP, Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd., Regarding Her Ongoing Attempt To Take The Apex Program’s CompTIA Network+ Exam at a Pearson Vue Testing Center As A Blind Woman in Canada | August 17, 2026

In this candid and unusually raw episode of Remarkable World Commentary, Donna J. Jodhan hands the microphone to her friend, associate and longtime collaborator Aaron Di Blasi for what he calls a “reverse grilling”, a date-by-date walk through her two-year attempt to sit the CompTIA Network+ exam as a blind candidate. Beginning with the $7,500 Apex Program scholarship awarded in November 2024, they trace a scholarship that turned out to be 21 typo-riddled Word documents with no learning platform and no human support; a first exam abandoned in October 2025 when the reader said “I don’t know what to do here”; the articles Donna published and the scholarship Apex withdrew because of them, telling her “you’ve made us the enemy”; the CNIB stepping in twice; and a second exam in May 2026 where the diagrams were still undescribed, the reader and recorder were one person, and her printed results had to be read aloud to her by a friend in the parking lot.

C.) Young Disabled People Across Europe Face Toxicity and Hostility From Disability Movement Veterans, Says Book | DisabilityNewsService.com | August 13, 2026

Dr Miro Griffiths’ book, “Youth, Disability, and Resistance,” finds that young disabled activists across the UK and Europe frequently face dismissal and hostility from veteran members of the disability movement. Based on surveys and interviews with over 200 young disabled people, Griffiths documents widespread gatekeeping, ageism, and barriers such as inaccessible venues and lack of support. He argues their full inclusion is vital for the movement’s future impact.

D.) Airline Disability Rules Delayed Again | DisabilityScoop.com | August 14, 2026

Federal officials have postponed enforcement of key provisions in the 2024 Wheelchair Rule, which was set to strengthen protections for airline passengers with disabilities. The US Department of Transportation will continue not enforcing requirements on staff training frequency, airline liability, passenger notification, and reimbursement for higher fares until at least April 30, 2027, as it considers revisions.

E.) Doctors, Advocates Call Out Trump For Claims About Autism | DisabilityScoop.com | August 12, 2026

President Donald Trump signed an executive order recommending reductions and wider spacing in childhood vaccines, citing rising autism rates as justification. Experts from the American Academy of Pediatrics and advocacy groups criticized the move, noting decades of research have found no link between vaccines and autism. The Autism Science Foundation highlighted genetic causes and said the science is settled.

August 24, 2026 📅️

2.) Access Information News Welcomes Derek Fine and Luna AI | Aaron Di Blasi, Publisher | August 24, 2026

Please join me in giving a warm welcome to Derek Fine and Luna AI, who has so very graciously agreed to support the ongoing distribution of Access Information News via sponsorship. If you enjoy reading Access Information News for free each week, it is Sponsors like Derek Fine and Luna AI that make it possible. And as I always say, these are the people, businesses and organizations that deserve your attention. Because they are the ones paying attention to the needs of the disability community. Luna AI is a voice-first tutor you reach by making an ordinary telephone call. Dial +1 (231) 879-5862 📱️ from any phone anywhere in the world, or use WhatsApp at the same number, and a conversational AI answers and starts teaching: it explains a concept out loud, quizzes you on it, listens to your answer in your own words, and corrects you when you get it wrong. Load your own lecture notes, transcripts, PDFs or a Quizlet set into a Study Library first, and the session comes out of your material rather than out of whatever an AI happens to know. There is no app, no account, no smartphone requirement, and no screen anywhere in the process, which also means no screen reader dependency, because there is no screen in the loop at all. Calling is free and there is no paywall. Founded in January 2026 by Derek Fine, Luna AI is new, small and has no published accessibility audit yet, so our suggestion is simple: call it once and form your own opinion.

3.) Call Luna. Learn Anything: Meet Derek Fine and Luna AI, Now Sponsoring Access Information News | AccessInformationNews.com | August 24, 2026

Luna AI, founded by Derek Fine in January 2026, enables users to access an AI tutor by simply calling +1 (231) 879-5862, requiring no app, account, or screen interaction. The phone-based conversational AI offers spoken study sessions using both general and user-uploaded materials, and remains free to use as of August 2026. Fine, with a background in travel marketing, plans a paid Luna AI Pro tier in 2027 but currently operates Luna solo as an early-stage project.

4.) RESIST! We Have Inherited a Legacy. Now It Is Our Turn. | Dr. Kirk Adams | August 24, 2026

Here, Dr. Kirk Adams invites readers to the free livestreamed launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, from 11:00 a.m. to noon Pacific (2:00 to 3:00 p.m. Eastern), and argues that the Coalition is inheriting a legacy rather than inventing one. Writing from a visit to Oakland in the Black Panther Party’s sixtieth anniversary year, he looks past the iconography to the Party’s Community Survival Programs, the free breakfasts, health clinics, sickle-cell testing, legal services and support for seniors and disabled people, and draws out the line that anchors the piece: resistance isn’t only about what we stand against, it is about what we build together.

August 22, 2026 📅️

5.) Newsletter | August 2026 | InclusiveImagination.co | August 22, 2026

Inclusive Imagination launches Chasing Rainbows ICG, a $19.99 braille-accessible card game featuring UV tactile illustrations, and kicks off its first Tabletop RPG Pre-ETS group in partnership with Washington State’s Department of Services for the Blind. A 20% back-to-school discount is available until September 15 using code BACK2SCHOOL. Updates for the Access Arcade App are also announced.

August 21, 2026 📅️

6.) Cooking After Vision Loss | HadleyHelps.org | August 21, 2026

Hadley Presents host Ricky Enger interviews Dia Kraft and Don Pojman, who share practical techniques for maintaining independence and safety in the kitchen after vision loss. The discussion details their personal adaptation strategies, favorite kitchen tools, and approaches to organization, highlighting the importance of customized workflows and resilience.

7.) When Money Talks – No Shocker or Shaker | BarrierFreeCanada.org | August 21, 2026

Facing legal disputes against institutions or governments often reveals a major imbalance: organizations with significant resources can prolong proceedings, while individuals may be pressured into settlements by mounting costs and delays. The piece questions whether Canada’s justice system truly offers equal access when outcomes depend on financial stamina.

8.) Hikers Who Use Wheelchairs Explore the Outdoors, Watching Out for One Another | DisabilityScoop.com | August 21, 2026

Oregon Wheelchair Hiking, founded in 2020 by Franklin Ouchida, has grown from four friends to a Facebook community of more than 600, regularly traversing wheelchair-accessible trails around Portland. Members like Heidi Austin and Vanessa Rice cite the group as key in making outdoor adventures feasible, while Ouchida collaborates with local agencies to improve trail accessibility and safety for participants.

9.) Kids With Cerebral Palsy Diagnosed at Younger Ages, CDC Finds | DisabilityScoop.com | August 21, 2026

A CDC study found that children born in 2018 with cerebral palsy were more likely to be diagnosed by age 4 than those born in 2014, based on data from nearly 215,000 children across five states. Prevalence rates reached 2.4 per 1,000 at age 8 and 2.2 per 1,000 at age 4. Black children were more likely than white children to have cerebral palsy and less likely to walk independently.

10.) What It’s Really Like Being A Single Mom Of An Autistic Daughter With Moderate Support Needs | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | August 21, 2026

Sitting down for an unfiltered conversation, Molly Burke interviews Christine Romeo about the lived realities of raising Abbey, her autistic daughter featured on Netflix’s Love on the Spectrum. Burke explores Christine’s journey from the initial diagnosis through to adulthood, highlighting the nuanced challenges and unexpected growth that shape their mother-daughter relationship.

August 20, 2026 📅️

11.) Podcasts By Dr. Kirk Adams: Interview With Tom Babinszki, Owner, Even Grounds | DrKirkAdams.com | August 20, 2026

Tom Babinszki, blind since birth and founder of Even Grounds, shares how his company delivers accessibility consulting and tactile 3D models to institutions like the Toledo Zoo, the Detroit Symphony Orchestra, and global schools for the blind. In conversation with Dr. Kirk Adams, Babinszki notes the impact of tactile restroom maps and advises never to accept inaccessibility as inevitable.

12.) Innovation for Access: AI and Its Use as Assistive Technology for People With Disabilities | AFB.org | August 20, 2026

A 2026 report from the American Foundation for the Blind presents survey data from 1,735 U.S. adults on how AI-powered visual descriptions, captions, and AAC tools are used as assistive technology. Key findings indicate high daily reliance on AI among blind, low-vision, and D/HH users, growing demand for greater accuracy, better privacy controls, and interface accessibility, and specific recommendations for inclusive AI development and responsible data practices.

13.) Beyond the Deadline: Counties Make Digital Accessibility an Everyday Practice | ConduitStreet.mdcounties.org | August 20, 2026

At the 2026 MACo Summer Conference, Delegate Pamela Queen and panelists Emily Lucht and Marshall Haas emphasized that digital accessibility for counties is an ongoing process rather than a completed task. Lucht outlined the importance of meaningful alt text, captions, and accessible documents, while Haas described how Queen Anne’s County embeds accessibility in staff training and workflows. Both highlighted starting with high-profile content and building sustainable practices.

14.) Here’s Your Guide to Accessibility in OKC’s Arts Institutions | FreePressOkc.com | August 20, 2026

Oklahoma City arts organizations including Factory Obscura, Oklahoma City Museum of Art, First Americans Museum, Civic Center Foundation, and Oklahoma Contemporary Arts Center are adopting new accessibility measures ranging from wheelchair availability and sensory kits to ASL interpretation and audio descriptions. Leaders such as Erin Schalk document how disability representation and direct engagement inform evolving practices aimed at making arts spaces more inclusive. Challenges persist, but ongoing efforts are prioritizing lived experience and continual adaptation.

15.) States Are Moving on Accessibility but Struggling, Say Digital Officers | StateScoop.com | August 20, 2026

A National Association of State Chief Information Officers survey of 36 state digital accessibility officers reveals that while digital accessibility leadership is becoming standard, most states lack the staff, authority, and funding to meet DOJ compliance deadlines. Only 17% of leads have oversight across all agencies, and 69% say they cannot remediate all sites and apps by next April.

16.) ‘We Have Nowhere to Go’: WV Handicap-Accessible Housing in Short Supply for Low-Income Residents | WestVirginiaWatch.com | August 20, 2026

Facing deteriorating living conditions, Sarah and Ricky Mathes are among many West Virginians with disabilities unable to secure accessible, affordable housing due to a severe shortage of suitable units. Public housing waiting lists can last up to six years, and only a small percentage of units are equipped for people with mobility needs. Local experts warn the situation is worsening as federally subsidized housing stock is projected to decline.

17.) NASCIO Looks In on State Digital Accessibility Officers | GovTech.com | August 20, 2026

A new NASCIO survey finds state digital accessibility officers are gaining traction but face persistent gaps in funding, staffing, and authority. Only 17 percent have authority across all agencies, and 67 percent of states lack a dedicated accessibility budget. AI use remains limited as executives mostly support accessibility efforts, but resource and process challenges hinder full compliance with DOJ rules.

18.) Bill Seeks to Increase Accessible LIHTC Developments | HousingFinance.com | August 20, 2026

Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Visitable Inclusive Tax Credits for Accessible Living (VITAL) Act to expand accessible housing for older adults and people with disabilities. The bill would increase state low-income housing tax credit allocations, add a basis boost for qualifying projects, and incentivize states to prioritize more accessible, walkable affordable housing. Companion legislation was also introduced in the House.

19.) Missing Elevator at Finch West Station Creates Uphill Battle for Transit Riders With Disabilities | InsideHalton.com | August 20, 2026

A newly opened Toronto light rail station lacks an elevator for riders with disabilities to transfer between intersecting lines, forcing them to use a 261-foot ramp that is longer than a 747 jet. Accessibility advocate David Lepofsky criticizes the Ontario government and Metrolinx, citing insufficient accessibility regulations and calling for an independent audit of transit designs.

20.) Contributor: Stop Shaming the Use of AI. For Some With Disabilities, It’s a Godsend | LATimes.com | August 20, 2026

Sharon Schindel challenges blanket condemnations of AI writing tools, arguing that for people with physical disabilities, AI can provide critical accessibility. She describes dictating her work due to severe arm pain and using AI only to clean up transcription debris, not to generate content. Schindel notes that 1 in 4 U.S. adults have a disability and stresses that universal prohibitions on AI risk excluding many voices.

21.) Poor Website Accessibility Could Exclude Persons With Disabilities From Essential Services | MyJoyOnline.com | August 20, 2026

At a workshop by Open Knowledge Ghana and the Internet Society Ghana Chapter, participants highlighted that poorly designed websites present significant barriers for persons with disabilities in Ghana, limiting access to essential services. Disability advocates and experts, including Sayena Susu and Ephraim Tetteh, urged developers to engage directly with disabled users and follow web accessibility guidelines as more government services move online.

22.) They Grew Up With Disability Rights. Now, They’re Fighting To Keep Them | NPR.org | August 20, 2026

Cody and Kaleigh Brendle, part of the ADA generation, are challenging federal shifts that threaten community-based disability services for more than 8 million Americans. A recent DOJ memo and the Texas v. Kennedy case signal a reversal in long-standing integration mandates, prompting activists like Kaleigh to mobilize against the potential rollback of disability rights protections.

23.) The DWP Is Not Accessible to Many – Defeating Its Own Purpose | TheCanary.co | August 20, 2026

Claimant Daniel Harvey details systemic accessibility failures at the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), citing a July 2026 Timms Review finding that over 90% of Personal Independence Payment applicants reported negative experiences. An incident at Ipswich Job Centre underscored inadequate legal compliance and highlighted the impact of exclusionary practices on disabled individuals.

Those include the ETIB Experience, an interview podcast featuring blind entrepreneurs, artists, advocates and pageant titleholders; ETIB Radio, an internet stream that gives independent blind and visually impaired musicians genuine airplay; the Community Connect Directory, a staff-verified listing of businesses that are blind-owned, visually-impaired-owned, or that specifically serve blind and low vision people; Seen Through Sound, a community project collecting short recorded messages of encouragement; plus a blog and an events calendar. Bussey founded ETIB, in his words, to help people feel “visible, connected, informed, and empowered without using pity as the message.”
