item.title: Call Luna. Learn Anything: Meet Derek Fine and Luna AI, Now Sponsoring Access Information News
item.dc:creator: Access Information News
item.description:
Here, Aaron Di Blasi, Publisher for the Access Information News weekly newsletter, introduces Luna AI, the publication's newest Sponsor, and the person who built it. Luna AI is an AI tutor you reach by making an ordinary telephone call. There is no app to download, no account to create before you can hear anything, no smartphone requirement, and no screen anywhere in the process. You dial the number, or reach the same service on WhatsApp, and a tutor answers: it explains a concept out loud, asks you about it, listens to your answer in your own words, and tells you when you have it wrong. Load your own lecture notes, transcripts, PDFs or a Quizlet set into a Study Library first, and the session comes out of your material rather than out of whatever an AI happens to know. Calling is free, there is no paywall, and every caller has access to the full product, with a paid Luna AI Pro tier planned for 2027.

The post Call Luna. Learn Anything: Meet Derek Fine and Luna AI, Now Sponsoring Access Information News appeared first on Access Information News.
item.content:encoded:
Access Information News has a new Sponsor, and the fastest way to understand what it does is to pick up a phone and dial +1 (231) 879-5862 📱️.

Pick up a phone. Any phone, the one in your pocket, the one on the kitchen wall, a handset you borrowed from someone in a hotel lobby. Dial +1 (231) 879-5862 📱️.

A conversational AI answers, and is ready to teach you.

That’s the whole of it. Luna AI at https://trylunaai.com is the newest sponsor of Access Information News, and it is a tutor you reach by making an ordinary telephone call. There’s no app to download, no account to create before you can hear anything, no smartphone requirement, and, perhaps most important to many AIN readers, no screen anywhere in the process.

We’re used to accessible technology meaning software that someone has carefully built to work well with a screen reader. This is a different proposition altogether. There is nothing on screen to read, because the interaction never touches a screen at all. A refreshingly different and intriguing paradigm if you ask me.

What Actually Happens When You Call?

Luna is a tutor, not a recording.

Ask it to explain something and it explains, out loud, in ordinary conversational speech. Then it asks you about what it just said. You answer, speaking, in your own words, and it responds to what you actually told it. Get something wrong and it tells you, then comes back at the same idea from a different direction.

The rhythm is closer to a study session with a patient friend than to an audiobook or a podcast. You talk. It listens. It pushes.

If you would rather not use the phone network, the same service answers on WhatsApp at the same number, which for readers outside the United States will often be the cheaper route.

Luna AI markets five uses on its website: practicing a language conversationally, learning practical step-by-step skills, preparing for exams, studying during a commute, and studying while walking or at the gym. What those have in common becomes obvious once they are listed together, every one is a situation where your eyes and hands are already busy, or where a screen was never going to be part of it.

The Study Library

A general-purpose assistant can tell you about photosynthesis. What it cannot do is quiz you on the specific eleven pages your instructor actually assigned.

That is what the Study Library is for. Before you call, you load your own material into it, lecture notes, transcripts, PDF uploads, or a link to a Quizlet set you already made. When you phone in, the session comes out of your material rather than out of the general pool of things an AI happens to know.

This is the difference between a system that knows things and a system that knows your syllabus, and for a student it is most of the difference that matters. The questions are drawn from what you will actually be tested on, in the vocabulary your course actually uses.

It also means the value compounds. A Study Library you have been feeding since January is worth considerably more in April than it was when you started.

Why The Phone Call Is The Interesting Part

It is worth sitting with the phone call for a moment, because it is doing more work than it first appears.

A phone call has no installation. No account setup before first use. No updates, no app store, no data plan, no compatibility matrix, no minimum operating system version, and no release that quietly breaks something that worked perfectly well last week.

And it has no screen reader dependency, not because someone did excellent work making it screen-reader friendly, but because there is no screen in the loop for a screen reader to read.

That set of absences matters most to precisely the people who are usually last in line. It works on a feature phone. It works on a landline. It works on a phone you borrowed. And it works for someone who has already bounced off three well-meaning accessible apps and has run out of appetite for a fourth.

There is a second thing worth noticing. Being asked a question out loud, answering it out loud, and being corrected out loud is a genuinely different cognitive act from reading a page over and over again. Pulling something out of memory under a little pressure is harder than recognizing it on a page, and the difficulty is the point. Luna’s format makes that the default mode rather than an optional extra you have to remember to do.

Who Built It?

Luna AI Is The Work of Derek Fine, who founded it in January 2026.

Fine is not from the assistive technology world, and it is worth being straightforward about that from the outset. His career is in travel. He studied marketing and economics at the University of San Diego, and has spent roughly seven years at The Travel Corporation, the group behind Trafalgar, Insight Vacations, Costsaver, Contiki and Uniworld, where he is currently Affiliate Manager and built the company’s affiliate marketing department from the ground up.

Alongside that he hosts the Travel to Profit podcast, a show about monetisation, distribution and the creator economy in travel. He also holds a certificate in artificial intelligence business strategy from UC Berkeley Executive Education, delivered through Emeritus, a business programme rather than an engineering one, a distinction he draws himself.

So, a partnership and performance marketer, based in Newport Beach, California, who has spent his professional life on the commercial side of a large travel group.

That is an unusual place for an assistive technology product to come from. It is also, in fairness, exactly the sort of place the phone-call idea might come from, someone whose whole job is distribution, asking why a product needs an app at all.

Why A Travel Marketer Built A Study Tool

Luna AI is not the first thing Fine has built on the side. He launched Offer Alert, a monetisation tool for social media creators, in December 2024. The pattern is a working marketer who builds products in the evenings.

His day job has produced results that stand up independently. He worked on the Trafalgar Travel partnership with Capital One Ad Solutions that won Best Travel and Hospitality Partnership at the 2026 US Partnership Awards, a campaign credited with 161 per cent year-over-year fourth-quarter revenue growth.

That award belongs to the campaign and the team behind it rather than to any one person. But it establishes something relevant: he has shipped commercial work at a scale that outside judges thought was the best in its category.

What he has not yet built is a track record in blindness technology. Luna AI is his first attempt at it.

What It Costs

Nothing. Calling Luna is free, there is no paywall, and every caller has access to the full product.

Fine tells us a paid tier, Luna AI Pro, is planned for 2027. He describes it as adding more study minutes per month and better personalization, including more flexibility in the material you can upload. Pricing has not been announced, and there is nothing to buy today.

So there is no institutional pricing, no site license and no education tier either, because there is nothing to purchase at all. You dial the number and you use it.

What Luna AI Is Not

I want to be straight with you about the scale of what you are looking at, because you’ll find out anyway and it’s better coming from me.

Luna AI is eight months old. It was founded in January 2026. It is currently one person, Derek Fine, working on it alongside a full-time job. There is no team page because there does not appear to be a team.

There is no published accessibility audit, no conformance report, and no documented testing with JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver or TalkBack that we were able to find. The website makes accessibility claims. We are not in a position to confirm them, so we are not repeating them here.

None of that is an accusation. Nearly every useful thing in this field started as one person with an idea (Top Tech Tidbits, Access Information News) and several of the tools our readers now rely on daily began in this exact way.

It is simply an honest description of what you are being introduced to: an early, small, genuinely interesting product, at the stage where it still has to prove itself.

Where It Sits Beside What You Already Use

Luna AI is another way in. It is not a replacement for the way you already work.

A fluent screen reader user reads far faster than any voice can speak. Braille and keyboard workflows remain the serious tools for serious study, and a student doing close work on a dense text is not going to be better served by linear speech. Anyone telling you that blind people should use voice instead of screens is selling something.

The case for Luna AI is narrower and more honest than that. It is for the times when a screen is not available, not convenient, or not wanted: the walk, the commute, the gym, the kitchen, the borrowed phone, the twenty minutes you would rather not waste.

Judged as a replacement for your existing setup, it will disappoint you. Judged as one more way in, available at no cost to try, it is worth ten minutes of your time.

How To Try It

Simply call +1 (231) 879-5862 📱️ from any phone, anywhere in the world. The same service answers on WhatsApp at the same number.

The website is https://trylunaai.com, where you can set up a Study Library and read the current Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs).

Our recommendation is simple. Call it once, before you read anything else about it, and form your own opinion. It costs nothing, it takes five minutes, and you are far better qualified than anyone else to judge whether it fits the way you actually study.

Welcome

Luna AI joined Access Information News as a Sponsor on August 16, 2026, and we are grateful to have them on board.

A word about what that means, since we are asked. Access Information News is a not-for-profit publication. Every dollar from sponsors, supporters and advertisers is held in escrow and used only to fund the ongoing distribution of each newsletter to more than 45,000 readers each week. When sponsorship packages go unfilled, my company, Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd., donates the difference to keep them running.

In short, if you enjoy reading Access Information News for free each and every week, it is Sponsors like Derek Fine and Luna AI that make it possible. And as I always say, these are the people, businesses and organizations that deserve your time and attention. Because they’re paying attention. To the needs of the disability community specifically.

Thank you Derek. Thank you Luna AI. We couldn’t do this without your support.

Sponsors provide much-needed support in exchange for verified, measurable reach. They cannot buy our editorial judgement. This article was written from an objective point of view based on the current market.

Welcome aboard, Luna AI. Thank you so much for your support.

” The greatest barrier to accessibility is indifference. “

Aaron Di Blasi, PMP
Engineer, Educator, Advocate, Publisher & Journalist
President & Sr. PMP, Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd., PR Director: AT-Newswire, Publisher: AI-Weekly, Top Tech Tidbits, Access Information News, Title II Today

Aaron Di Blasi is a computer engineer, marketing strategist and publisher, and one of the world’s leading voices at the intersection of artificial intelligence, marketing, and accessibility. A computer engineer (Case Western Reserve University / 1998) who began his career building digital products for the American Machinist and Machine Design magazines in downtown Cleveland, Ohio, Aaron Di Blasi (https://www.linkedin.com/in/aarondiblasi/) has spent more than 25 years in technology and digital media and more than two decades serving the blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and disabled communities. Aaron Di Blasi is the founder and President of Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. (https://mvsltd.com), an award-winning international provider of cutting-edge automation and artificial intelligence-enhanced digital marketing services, and a PMP-certified Senior Project Management Professional. Aaron Di Blasi is also the founder and PR Director for the AT-Newswire Press Release News Distribution Service (https://at-newswire.com), the world’s only press release distribution service dedicated to serving the blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and disabled communities. Aaron Di Blasi possesses a deep, technical, hands-on expertise in artificial intelligence, particularly where AI intersects with automation, digital marketing and accessibility. Aaron Di Blasi’s expertise includes, but is not limited to, natural language processing (NLP), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), computer vision, generative AI, AI-assisted content aggregation and curation, AI workflows and process automation (including platforms such as https://make.com), AI in marketing, AI in publishing, and AI for strategy. ♿️ The Week’s News in Access Information

Access Information News. The world’s #1 online resource for current news and trends in access information.

A Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. Publication

Subscribers:  47,126 🔢️ opt-in subscribers were sent this issue via email.

Social Media:  191,488 🔢️ readers were sent this issue via social media, courtesy of the PWD Media Distribution Co-Op.

Share: Facebook | X (Twitter) | LinkedIn | Email | Web Link | How to read this newsletter if you are blind or low-vision.

Section Jumper: Sponsors | Access Awareness | Featured Advertisement | News | Featured Events | Classified Ads | Supporters | News Team | Subscription Information

Sponsors 🏅️

Access Awareness: Updates That Matter ♿️

Recruiting College Talent With Disabilities: What Works, What Doesn’t, And Why | National Organization on Disability | YouTube.com | August 13, 2026

In this analytical framing, National Organization on Disability closely examines the persistent hurdles recruiters face when engaging college students with disabilities. Supported by recent NOD research, the session highlights concrete steps for improving campus connections and creating accessible environments where early-career professionals can succeed.

This Week’s Featured Advertisement ️

Sponsorship Packages Currently Available: Join Industry Leaders in Supporting Free Access Information News For Disabled Readers All Over The World While Increasing Traffic To Your Properties Each Week. Advertise in every issue. Or just one.

Join Access Information News as a Sponsor today and begin reaching over 45,000 access information readers each week, all while supporting the ongoing distribution of Access Information News for those very same readers. Only $200 / month.

Key Newsletter Statistics:

  • Subscribers: 45,000 + per week and growing.
  • Open Rate: 47% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Click Rate: 34% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Bounce Rate: 1.2% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Ad CTRs: 2-12% (Average. Last 12 months.)

Benefits All Sponsors Receive:

  • One (1) Sponsor Profile on the Access Information News website, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Profile in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement on the Access Information News home page + every page of the website (Right Side Bar: Sponsors), for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Classified Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Membership in the PWD Media Co-Op, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • 50% Discount on all Sponsored News Article Advertisements, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Free link tracking, for all time.
  • Permanent SEO benefits. (All Sponsor Profiles are archived on the Access Information News website at the close of Sponsorship. Driving traffic back to your properties for all time.
  • Gratitude from over 45,000 blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled professionals, educators, and enthusiasts, all over the world, along with the caregivers, companies and organizations that serve and support them, for keeping Access Information News free to read each week.

With additional benefits for Sponsors who choose to pay quarterly or annually. Learn more about Sponsorship today. today.

News 📰️

👉 Submit a news article for free here, with timing and placement determined by our editors.

👉 Submit a Sponsored News Article here, with timing and placement determined by you.

1.) Top 5 Most Clicked News Articles From Last Week 📊️

A.) Can You Raise Children Without Screens Anymore? | Jessica Kellgren-Fozard | YouTube.com | August 5, 2026

Cutting through the hype around modern parenting, Jessica Kellgren-Fozard examines how families are navigating the realities of screens, algorithms, and digital education. She tackles questions on whether screen-free children are left behind, the complexities in schools’ approaches, and the rising need for critical digital literacy in an always-online world.

B.) Podcast: Driven By Purpose: Father and Son Built a Sock Empire to Prove the World Wrong | John’s Crazy Socks | By Isaac Shapiro of Cleanlogic and The Inspiration Foundation | August 10, 2026

In the fall of 2016, John Cronin was finishing high school and couldn’t find a job he liked. So he decided to make one. Nine years later, John’s Crazy Socks has shipped over 500,000 packages to 94 countries, donated more than $850,000 to charity, employed dozens of people with different abilities, and landed John on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list. Oh, and he’s become sock buddies with a former president. In this episode of Driven By Purpose, Evan Rosenblum and Isaac Shapiro sit down with John Cronin and his dad Mark X. Cronin, co-founders of John’s Crazy Socks. This is one of the most energetic, funny, and genuinely moving conversations the show has ever had. From delivering their first 42 orders by hand in red boxes with candy and lights, to testifying before Congress, to confronting The Rock publicly over the R word, John and Mark are as real as it gets.

C.) Part 4: My Experience Trying To Take the Apex Program’s CompTIA Network+ Exam at a Pearson Vue Testing Center As A Blind Woman in Canada | Donna J. Jodhan, LLB, ACSP, MBA | August 10, 2026

Here, Donna J. Jodhan returns to a Pearson Vue testing centre for a second attempt at the CompTIA Network+ exam, eight months after an inaccessible first sitting ended before it could begin. Pearson approved every accommodation she asked for and its staff treated her with real kindness, yet she met the same barrier that stopped her in October 2025: exam diagrams carrying no validated descriptions, improvised aloud by a reader who had never seen them. Along the way she was steered away from the JAWS screen reader she asked about, had her testing agreements recited to her because nobody mentioned they were available online to read herself, was given one person to perform two separately approved roles, and finally received her results on a sheet of paper she could not read. She did not pass, and she is candid about the cruelty at the heart of that: when the process is inaccessible, you never find out what you actually knew.

D.) Welcome, Even Though I’m Blind: Why Our Newest Sponsor Named His Organization After His Own Song | AccessInformationNews.com | August 5, 2026

Cazerny Bussey, a Brooklyn-born recording artist, founded Even Though I’m Blind, Inc. (ETIB) in 2025, naming the organization after his own song. ETIB now runs a radio station, podcast, vetted business directory, and community initiatives led by blind individuals, emphasizing lived experience over pity. Access Information News announced ETIB as its newest sponsor, highlighting the group’s early but impactful efforts in blind-led media.

E.) Why Some Americans Want to Be Disabled | TheDispatch.com | August 1, 2026

Jon Gingerich examines social and psychological factors behind the increasing phenomenon of Americans expressing a desire for disability identification. Drawing from personal experience with vision loss, he reflects on the concept of “luxury identities” and how changing attitudes toward disability are shaping both individual self-perception and broader cultural trends.

August 17, 2026 📅️

2.) Podcast: Remarkable World Commentary Episode #102: Interview with Aaron Di Blasi, Sr. PMP, Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd., Regarding Her Ongoing Attempt To Take The Apex Program’s CompTIA Network+ Exam at a Pearson Vue Testing Center As A Blind Woman in Canada | August 17, 2026

In this candid and unusually raw episode of Remarkable World Commentary, Donna J. Jodhan hands the microphone to her friend, associate and longtime collaborator Aaron Di Blasi for what he calls a “reverse grilling”, a date-by-date walk through her two-year attempt to sit the CompTIA Network+ exam as a blind candidate. Beginning with the $7,500 Apex Program scholarship awarded in November 2024, they trace a scholarship that turned out to be 21 typo-riddled Word documents with no learning platform and no human support; a first exam abandoned in October 2025 when the reader said “I don’t know what to do here”; the articles Donna published and the scholarship Apex withdrew because of them, telling her “you’ve made us the enemy”; the CNIB stepping in twice; and a second exam in May 2026 where the diagrams were still undescribed, the reader and recorder were one person, and her printed results had to be read aloud to her by a friend in the parking lot.

August 15, 2026 📅️

3.) Locking Lid Pan | The Blind Kitchen | YouTube.com | August 15, 2026

Showcasing accessible kitchen solutions, The Blind Kitchen introduces the locking lid pan and demonstrates how its unique handle design streamlines straining for cooks with vision loss. Instead of juggling boiling water and searching for a colander, the secure lid and dual spouts make draining safely manageable and efficient.

August 14, 2026 📅️

4.) I Shouldn’t Have to Fight for Dignity Every Time I Get on a Plane | HumanRights.gov.au | August 14, 2026

Disability Discrimination Commissioner Rosemary Kayess argues that new Australian aviation disability standards are a rare opportunity to enforce accessible air travel for people with disabilities. Kayess, drawing from her personal experience, outlines persistent barriers and calls for enforceable standards, consistent pre-approval for mobility devices, staff training, and robust data reporting to ensure dignity and universal access.

5.) Airline Disability Rules Delayed Again | DisabilityScoop.com | August 14, 2026

Federal officials have postponed enforcement of key provisions in the 2024 Wheelchair Rule, which was set to strengthen protections for airline passengers with disabilities. The US Department of Transportation will continue not enforcing requirements on staff training frequency, airline liability, passenger notification, and reimbursement for higher fares until at least April 30, 2027, as it considers revisions.

6.) Missoula Neighbors United Holds Accessibility Audit for West Broadway Corridor | KPAX.com | August 14, 2026

Missoula Neighbors United conducted an accessibility audit of the West Broadway corridor, pairing residents with disabilities and city planners to evaluate sidewalks and safety needs. City transportation planner Ben Weiss outlined scoring criteria including sidewalk adequacy, destination access, site design, and overall accessibility. Insights from residents at ten locations will inform future infrastructure decisions.

7.) NCDA Supports Proposed Bills Guaranteeing Monthly Allowance, Digital Accessibility for PWDs | ManilaTimes.net | August 14, 2026

The National Council on Disability Affairs has endorsed legislative measures in the Philippines that would grant qualified persons with disabilities a P2,000 monthly allowance, as detailed in Senate Bill No. 2386. Separate bills in the House target digital accessibility, aiming to eliminate online barriers for people with impairments and ensure unrestricted access to digital services.

8.) Students In Special Education Find Hope With School Vouchers, But Face Obstacles | DisabilityScoop.com | August 14, 2026

While Texas’ new Education Freedom Accounts offer up to $30,000 in vouchers for students with disabilities, families like the Howks and Danisha Nunn report persistent barriers as private school tuition often outpaces awards and many schools limit admissions. Critics warn students risk losing legal protections, while some families are forced to settle for homeschooling or compromise on chosen schools.

9.) What It’s Really Like When Your Disability Is Someone’s Fetish | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | August 14, 2026

Sitting down with the realities of disability, Molly Burke leads an open, forthright discussion with Tara Shetterly about the complexities of life after paralysis, relationships, and the troubling phenomenon of disability fetishization. Their conversation surfaces the rarely heard challenges of dating, identity, and self-advocacy in a world not designed for disabled voices. Burke brings nuance and candor to topics of love, ableism, and personal resilience throughout this episode.

August 13, 2026 📅️

10.) Churches Say They’re Welcoming to Those With Disabilities | MinistryWatch.com | August 13, 2026

A Lifeway Research survey finds that 98% of U.S. Protestant pastors and churchgoers believe people with disabilities would feel welcomed in their churches, but confidence has declined since 2019. While most pastors say their churches make facility modifications and offer financial or volunteer support, gaps remain in preparedness and inclusivity across different types of disabilities.

11.) Visually Impaired Secret Shoppers Put Edinburgh Festival Fringe Accessibility to the Test | Thiis.co.uk | August 13, 2026

Visually impaired volunteers from Sight Loss Councils Scotland are conducting secret visits at Edinburgh Festival Fringe venues to evaluate accessibility progress. Engagement Manager Callum Lancashire reports notable improvements due to targeted training but emphasizes that venues must continue prioritizing inclusion year-round. Colette Walker, Co-Chair of Sight Scotland’s Policy Group, underscores the need for clear information, staff awareness, and seamless support for disabled audiences.

12.) New Colorado Law Expands Disability Protections for Students Amid Federal Education Changes | CBSNews.com | August 13, 2026

Colorado’s SB26-125 bans public schools from discriminating against students with disabilities, mandating equal access and reasonable accommodations. Prompted partly by federal education changes and Department of Education restructuring under the Trump administration, the law establishes state-level oversight, grievance procedures, and new enforcement powers. Advocates such as Pam Bisceglia of Advocacy Denver cite slow federal complaint processes as a key driver.

13.) Young Disabled People Across Europe Face Toxicity and Hostility From Disability Movement Veterans, Says Book | DisabilityNewsService.com | August 13, 2026

Dr Miro Griffiths’ book, “Youth, Disability, and Resistance,” finds that young disabled activists across the UK and Europe frequently face dismissal and hostility from veteran members of the disability movement. Based on surveys and interviews with over 200 young disabled people, Griffiths documents widespread gatekeeping, ageism, and barriers such as inaccessible venues and lack of support. He argues their full inclusion is vital for the movement’s future impact.

14.) ADA Expansion Brings New Accessibility Requirements to Government Websites | KIVITV.com | August 13, 2026

New federal Americans with Disabilities Act rules now require state and local governments to update websites, social media, and mobile apps for accessibility. Katie Warden of the Northwest ADA Center emphasizes that digital content must meet standards like screen reader compatibility and color contrast. Cities such as Boise have until April 2027 to comply, while smaller communities have until April 2028.

15.) Nonprofit Helps Adults With Disabilities Gain Job Skills as Repair Technicians | DisabilityScoop.com | August 13, 2026

Jonathan’s Landing Foundation launched the Techtonic initiative with $1.75 million in state funding, training adults with autism and other disabilities to repair electronics and gain industry credentials. CEO Kimberly McCarten and founder Jason Eichenholz aim to expand from their Winter Park, Fla. facility, despite a recent $750,000 funding veto by Gov. Ron DeSantis.

16.) NCDA Calls for Stricter Compliance With Accessibility Law | Inquirer.net | August 13, 2026

The National Council on Disability Affairs urged both public and private establishments, as well as local government units, to intensify compliance with the Accessibility Law and the 2024 Revised IRR of Batas Pambansa Blg. 344. NCDA called for regular inspections and technical audits, emphasizing that accessibility features must fully meet legal standards to ensure safety and inclusion for persons with disabilities.

17.) Recruiting College Talent With Disabilities: What Works, What Doesn’t, And Why | National Organization on Disability | YouTube.com | August 13, 2026

In this analytical framing, National Organization on Disability closely examines the persistent hurdles recruiters face when engaging college students with disabilities. Supported by recent NOD research, the session highlights concrete steps for improving campus connections and creating accessible environments where early-career professionals can succeed.

18.) Handi-Link: Healthcare Reform, Employment, 22Q | Cam Wells | CJAM 99.1 FM | August 13, 2026

This program focuses on disability issues. Host Cam Wells will explore all sides of this comparing and contrasting with able bodied life. This week Featuring: Sean Wiltshire Avalon Employment. Janet Himmeroeder: 22Q advocate. Teri Mcgrath Healthcare Advocate.

August 12, 2026 📅️

19.) New Houses Must Be More Accessible for People With Special Needs | NewsERR.ee | August 12, 2026

Estonia has enacted new accessibility rules for residential buildings, requiring that, from January 2027, at least 10% of apartments in new developments be easily adaptable for people with special needs. Ministry of Climate official Ivo Jaanisoo emphasized accessibility should be fundamental, not an afterthought. Mari Tuulik of the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People stressed early involvement of disability organizations.

20.) When Disabled People Are Priced Out, We Lose More Than a Home | OtherWords.org | August 12, 2026

Disabled people, especially Black women like Janiah Miller in metro Atlanta, are being forced from their communities by rising housing and utility costs. These financial pressures not only disrupt the daily support networks crucial for independence and care but also expose policy gaps in accessibility. Miller asserts that true accessibility requires affordable housing, regulated utility billing, and protection of social infrastructure.

21.) Sight-Impaired Woman ‘Disempowered’ by Hospital During Pregnancy | BBC.com | August 12, 2026

Jenny Molineux, a visually impaired mother from Rawtenstall, said she felt “disempowered” when she could not access her own maternity records during her pregnancy at Lancashire Women & Newborn Centre. East Lancashire Hospital Trust has since introduced initiatives like accessible postnatal discharge videos and a dedicated information group, but Molineux notes these improvements came only after her experience.

22.) Accessibility Takes Center Stage at Epidaurus | EKathimerini.com | August 12, 2026

“The Trojan Women” at the ancient theater of Epidaurus featured Greece’s first universally accessible performance, with people with visual and hearing impairments provided tactile set models, audio description, and Greek Sign Language interpretation. Irini Kourouvani, a dancer in a wheelchair, and director Eleni Efthymiou emphasized that accessibility was integrated from the start rather than as an afterthought.

23.) Doctors, Advocates Call Out Trump For Claims About Autism | DisabilityScoop.com | August 12, 2026

President Donald Trump signed an executive order recommending reductions and wider spacing in childhood vaccines, citing rising autism rates as justification. Experts from the American Academy of Pediatrics and advocacy groups criticized the move, noting decades of research have found no link between vaccines and autism. The Autism Science Foundation highlighted genetic causes and said the science is settled.

24.) A New Addition to the Oregon Capitol Helps Children With Severe Disabilities Advocate With Dignity | OregonLive.com | August 12, 2026

A universal, motorized changing table for older children and adults with severe disabilities has been installed at the Oregon Capitol, the first dedicated space of its kind in the building after a nearly $600 million renovation. Disability advocates like Calli Ross highlighted the need for such a facility after families previously resorted to makeshift solutions, sparking calls for improved accessibility.

25.) Meet Shanna Chevalier, TDOT Statewide ADA Technical Specialist and U.S. Army Veteran | TNGov.com | August 12, 2026

Shanna Chevalier, Tennessee Department of Transportation’s Statewide ADA Technical Specialist and a U.S. Army veteran, coordinates accessibility compliance across TDOT projects and programs. Drawing on her military experience and over 10 years in Equal Opportunity, Chevalier emphasizes that accessibility requires active planning and department-wide collaboration, impacting both physical facilities and digital content.

26.) Liquid Alert Audio & Vibrating | The Blind Kitchen | YouTube.com | August 12, 2026

Showcasing the latest in accessible kitchen tools, The Blind Kitchen walks viewers through how Audio and Vibrating Liquid Alert devices help those with limited vision pour confidently and independently. From travel-friendly features to the dual alert systems that distinguish near-full from overflow, the episode highlights subtle innovations that directly address the challenges of daily living.

27.) Are Queer Dating Standards Too High? | Jessica Kellgren-Fozard | YouTube.com | August 12, 2026

Sitting down with candid questions from her audience, Jessica Kellgren-Fozard examines the realities and myths around expectations in queer dating. Bringing her trademark warmth and sharp perspective, Kellgren-Fozard addresses everything from second date nerves to the challenges of balancing family acceptance and personal standards.

August 11, 2026 📅️

28.) P.E.I.’s First Access Beach Day Spotlights Resources for Islanders With Disabilities | CBC.ca | August 11, 2026

ParaSport and Recreation P.E.I., in coordination with the Spinal Cord Injury Association of P.E.I. and Parks Canada, organized the first Access Beach Day at Stanhope Beach to demonstrate accessible equipment like floating wheelchairs and mobility mats. Program coordinator Craig MacDougall said such resources enable people with physical disabilities to fully experience P.E.I.’s beaches. Equipment, available at select beaches, must be reserved in advance through Parks Canada.

29.) Yale Study: Medicare for All Would Save Over 114,000 Lives and $1 Trillion a Year | CommonDreams.org | August 11, 2026

A new Yale University study estimates that implementing Medicare for All in the US would save over 114,000 lives and reduce national health expenditure by $1.04 trillion annually. Key areas of savings include lower drug costs, reduced bureaucracy and waste, and fewer avoidable emergency visits. Senator Bernie Sanders cited the findings as further evidence for universal healthcare adoption.

30.) Faith Beyond Words: How Bishop Chau Uses ASL to Make Catholicism More Accessible | TheSetonian.com | August 11, 2026

Bishop Pedro Bismarck Chau, auxiliary bishop of Newark and Seton Hall alumnus, uses American Sign Language (ASL) to bridge gaps for Deaf Catholics, inspired by his sister’s experience as a deaf woman in both Nicaragua and the US. Chau advocates integrating ASL training into seminary education, citing persistent challenges with accessibility and calling for greater inclusion within Catholic parishes.

31.) As Special Education Enrollment Rises, Schools Face Mounting Costs | DisabilityScoop.com | August 11, 2026

A surge in special education enrollment is forcing districts like South Park, Montour, and Moon Area to add staff, classrooms, and services, with costs rising by hundreds of thousands of dollars annually. Despite a $55 million boost to Pennsylvania’s special education budget in July 2026, district officials say funding still covers only a fraction of expenses, leaving local schools under continued fiscal pressure.

32.) Inclusive Fitness for Kids with Developmental Disabilities Is Gym’s Goal | DisabilityScoop.com | August 11, 2026

Kevin Quinn, owner of Quinn’s Gym in Carmichael, launched the RISE program to provide inclusive fitness classes for children and adults with developmental disabilities, including autism, Down syndrome, and cerebral palsy. The program uses play-based exercise to foster strength, confidence, and a sense of belonging among participants, with a high coach-to-child ratio and individualized support.

33.) These Places Banned Subminimum Wage. Here’s What Happened To Workers With Disabilities | DisabilityScoop.com | August 11, 2026

A first-of-its-kind analysis in Labour Economics found that banning subminimum wage in 15 states did not significantly reduce employment, hours, or wages for workers with disabilities. Economist Michelle Yin of Northwestern University reports that former sheltered workshop employees largely remained in the workforce, while income from government welfare declined more than 12 percent.

34.) Sylvia Stinson-Perez Camino De Santiago The Cooking Without Looking Podcast #ChangingTheWayWeSeeBlin | Cooking Without Looking | YouTube.com | August 11, 2026

Innovative ideas. Solutions that perform.

Editor (2020-Present)
Top Tech Tidbits 🌐
The Week’s News in Access Technology

Editor: David Woodbridge

Editor Since: February 6, 2023

Location: Central Coast, New South Wales, Australia

Time Zone: Australia Eastern Standard Time (AEST/AEDT) (GMT+10)

In addition to serving as an Editor to Access Information News David also serves as an Editor to the Top Tech Tidbits publication and is also the National Commercial Assistive Technology Advisor for Vision Australia where he has worked since 1990. Over this time he has assisted people who are blind or vision impaired in their home, education, and work settings to take advantage of the benefits of using assistive and main stream technology.

In the last seventeen years, he has also been involved with evaluating technology for use by people who are blind or vision impaired covering both low and high tech equipment (including Microsoft, Samsung, Google, Amazon, and Apple). David is also one of the key spokespersons for Vision Australia relating to technology.

He has been an Apple Ambassador for Apple Australia since 2009 with a group of other Ambassadors / Apple Distinguished Educators (ADE)‘s covering the range of Apple’s Accessibility solutions throughout Australia.

David produces a range of podcasts (since 2011) covering Apple and other technologies which are distributed on his own podcast (http://davidwoodbr.podbean.com). In addition, he also has a regular Talking Tech program (since 2013) which can be heard every Tuesday at 4:30 Eastern Summer Time on Vision Australia Radio Melbourne (available online) or via https://omny.fm/shows/talking-tech-vision-australia-radio

David also runs a weekly Tech Monday where people can chat about assistive and main stream technology, share information, and any tips and tricks.

David lost his sight when he was 8 years old and had to learn Braille. Since then, he completed high school, went to Sydney University receiving a Social Work degree, spent 4 years drug and alcohol counselling, and then moved into his current job.

As a person who is blind, David believes that as a user of the technology that he recommends to others, that he is well situated to look at the strengths and shortcomings of the assistive technology that he comes across in both his professional and personal life, in particular, mainstream technology that is accessible.

In addition to his weekly contributions to Access Information News and Top Tech Tidbits, David’s regularly occurring activities are his weekly tech radio show, bi-monthly exploring tech webinars for Vision Australia, his iSee podcast when something of note grabs his attention, and the weekly Tech Monday chat sessions.

David Woodbridge

ABOUT ♿️

Founded in 2022, Access Information News is the world’s leading not-for-profit access information news publication that reaches over 45,000 blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled professionals, educators and enthusiasts, all over the world, each week, along with the caregivers, companies and organizations that serve and support them. Subscribe here. Review the most recent issues here. Access Information refers to informational topics that directly affect the lives of people with disabilities. Access Information includes any and all information related to bettering the lives of people who are blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled. Access Information News is a Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. Publication. Publisher: Aaron Di Blasi. Editors: John Hanlin, Jenna Lang, David Woodbridge and Vicki Walton. Access Information News is a sponsor, reader and advertiser supported publication.

item.content:encoded:
♿️ The Week’s News in Access Information

Access Information News. The world’s #1 online resource for current news and trends in access information.

A Mind Vault Solutions, Ltd. Publication

Subscribers:  46,930 🔢️ opt-in subscribers were sent this issue via email.

Social Media:  190,488 🔢️ readers were sent this issue via social media, courtesy of the PWD Media Distribution Co-Op.

Share: Facebook | X (Twitter) | LinkedIn | Email | Web Link | How to read this newsletter if you are blind or low-vision.

Section Jumper: Sponsors | Access Awareness | Featured Advertisement | News | Featured Events | Classified Ads | Supporters | News Team | Subscription Information

Sponsors 🏅️

Access Awareness: Updates That Matter ♿️

Can You Raise Children Without Screens Anymore? | Jessica Kellgren-Fozard | YouTube.com | August 5, 2026

Cutting through the hype around modern parenting, Jessica Kellgren-Fozard examines how families are navigating the realities of screens, algorithms, and digital education. She tackles questions on whether screen-free children are left behind, the complexities in schools’ approaches, and the rising need for critical digital literacy in an always-online world.

This Week’s Featured Advertisement ️

Sponsorship Packages Currently Available: Join Industry Leaders in Supporting Free Access Information News For Disabled Readers All Over The World While Increasing Traffic To Your Properties Each Week. Advertise in every issue. Or just one.

Join Access Information News as a Sponsor today and begin reaching over 45,000 access information readers each week, all while supporting the ongoing distribution of Access Information News for those very same readers. Only $200 / month.

Key Newsletter Statistics:

  • Subscribers: 45,000 + per week and growing.
  • Open Rate: 47% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Click Rate: 34% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Bounce Rate: 1.2% (Average. Last 12 months.)
  • Ad CTRs: 2-12% (Average. Last 12 months.)

Benefits All Sponsors Receive:

  • One (1) Sponsor Profile on the Access Information News website, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Profile in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement on the Access Information News home page + every page of the website (Right Side Bar: Sponsors), for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Sponsor Wall Brand Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • One (1) Classified Advertisement in each weekly newsletter, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Membership in the PWD Media Co-Op, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • 50% Discount on all Sponsored News Article Advertisements, for the duration of your sponsorship.
  • Free link tracking, for all time.
  • Permanent SEO benefits. (All Sponsor Profiles are archived on the Access Information News website at the close of Sponsorship. Driving traffic back to your properties for all time.
  • Gratitude from over 45,000 blind, low vision, deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind, neurodivergent and/or disabled professionals, educators, and enthusiasts, all over the world, along with the caregivers, companies and organizations that serve and support them, for keeping Access Information News free to read each week.

With additional benefits for Sponsors who choose to pay quarterly or annually. See all Sponsor benefits.

News 📰️

👉 Submit a news article for free here, with timing and placement determined by our editors.

👉 Submit a Sponsored News Article here, with timing and placement determined by you.

1.) Top 5 Most Clicked News Articles From Last Week 📊️

A.) Pushback on Ed Department Plan to Offload Special Education Intensifies | DisabilityScoop.com | July 31, 2026

A bipartisan Senate committee vote is intensifying opposition to the Department of Education’s plan to shift responsibilities for special education to the Department of Health and Human Services. Lawmakers including Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, and Tim Kaine argue the move undermines congressional intent, as disability advocates and former officials warn of risks to students’ rights. Secretary Linda McMahon defends the transition as a commonsense partnership.

B.) AI Has Ideas About Intellectual Disabilities. It’s Not Always Accurate | DisabilityScoop.com | July 30, 2026

A new study by Special Olympics International and Oregon State University finds that leading AI models like ChatGPT and Claude often portray people with intellectual disabilities as dependent, childlike, and in need of supervision. Researchers analyzed 25,000 AI-generated stories, concluding that these patterns echo ableist stereotypes and risk perpetuating biased decision-making in areas like healthcare and employment.

C.) What It’s Really Like To Outlive Your Life Expectancy | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | July 31, 2026

Cutting through perceptions around rare disease, Molly Burke sits down with Roman Perkins to reveal what it means to outlive a childhood prognosis and build an independent life. Their conversation navigates hurdles from misdiagnosis and low expectations to the powerful role of advocacy, community, and representation for those living with disabilities.

D.) Care Left In Limbo Amid Medicaid Fraud Crackdown | DisabilityScoop.com | July 29, 2026

Following a Minnesota Department of Human Services (DHS) initiative to root out Medicaid fraud under federal pressure, thousands of social service providers were abruptly reviewed or disenrolled, placing critical services for adults with developmental disabilities in jeopardy. Over 2,730 organizations appealed, with only about 750 reinstated. The state faces uncertainty after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services withheld $199 million in payments.

E.) This Is Your Invitation: Help Build a Community Where Everyone Belongs | DrKirkAdams.com | July 30, 2026

Dr. Kirk Adams, Executive Director of the Institute for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion, calls for support to launch a Community Coalition focused on accessibility, belonging, and inclusion across diverse groups. The initiative aims to address isolation by providing a collaborative platform where individuals and leaders can connect, share resources, and foster equitable opportunities.

August 10, 2026 📅️

2.) Access Information News Welcomes Cazerny Bussey and Even Though I’m Blind (ETIB) | Aaron Di Blasi, Publisher | August 10, 2026

Please join me in giving a warm welcome to Cazerny Bussey and Even Though I’m Blind (ETIB), who has so very graciously agreed to support the ongoing distribution of Access Information News via Sponsorship. If you enjoy reading Access Information News for free each week, it is sponsors like Cazerny Bussey and Even Though I’m Blind (ETIB) that make it possible. And as I always say, these are the people, companies and organizations that deserve your time and attention. Why? Because everyone says they care about the needs of disbled readers, but only a select few prove it by actively helping to keep the publications you rely on funded. Even Though I’m Blind, Inc. (ETIB) is a blind-led media and advocacy organization founded by Cazerny Bussey, a Brooklyn-born recording artist, author, entrepreneur, speaker, and father of five who lost his eyesight at fifteen. The organization takes its name from a track on Bussey’s 2021 album Cfly 728, one of three records he has released since 2012. ETIB’s stated mission is to uplift blind and visually impaired people by creating platforms and experiences that inform, inspire, connect, and open doors, and it does so through a working set of properties rather than a single channel. Learn more about Cazerny and ETIB today, and please consider dropping them a thank you for keeping AIN free to read.

3.) Podcast: Driven By Purpose: Father and Son Built a Sock Empire to Prove the World Wrong | John’s Crazy Socks | By Isaac Shapiro of Cleanlogic and The Inspiration Foundation | August 10, 2026

In the fall of 2016, John Cronin was finishing high school and couldn’t find a job he liked. So he decided to make one. Nine years later, John’s Crazy Socks has shipped over 500,000 packages to 94 countries, donated more than $850,000 to charity, employed dozens of people with different abilities, and landed John on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list. Oh, and he’s become sock buddies with a former president. In this episode of Driven By Purpose, Evan Rosenblum and Isaac Shapiro sit down with John Cronin and his dad Mark X. Cronin, co-founders of John’s Crazy Socks. This is one of the most energetic, funny, and genuinely moving conversations the show has ever had. From delivering their first 42 orders by hand in red boxes with candy and lights, to testifying before Congress, to confronting The Rock publicly over the R word, John and Mark are as real as it gets.

4.) Title II Today: Compliance & Accessibility Insights for Monday, August 10, 2026 – Volume 118 | Title2.info | August 10, 2026

Here Aaron Di Blasi rounds up the month’s news in Title II compliance on behalf of Pneuma Solutions.

5.) Part 4: My Experience Trying To Take the Apex Program’s CompTIA Network+ Exam at a Pearson Vue Testing Center As A Blind Woman in Canada | Donna J. Jodhan, LLB, ACSP, MBA | August 10, 2026

Here, Donna J. Jodhan returns to a Pearson Vue testing centre for a second attempt at the CompTIA Network+ exam, eight months after an inaccessible first sitting ended before it could begin. Pearson approved every accommodation she asked for and its staff treated her with real kindness, yet she met the same barrier that stopped her in October 2025: exam diagrams carrying no validated descriptions, improvised aloud by a reader who had never seen them. Along the way she was steered away from the JAWS screen reader she asked about, had her testing agreements recited to her because nobody mentioned they were available online to read herself, was given one person to perform two separately approved roles, and finally received her results on a sheet of paper she could not read. She did not pass, and she is candid about the cruelty at the heart of that: when the process is inaccessible, you never find out what you actually knew.

August 9, 2026 📅️

6.) Giannoulias Launches Disability Parking Placard Pilot as New Law Expands Access for Caregivers | RiverBender.com | August 9, 2026

Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias introduced a pilot program expanding disability parking placard services, following the signing of House Bill 4843. The law, effective immediately, allows legal guardians to obtain meter-exempt placards for individuals with disabilities who cannot drive, streamlining access at 14 additional facilities statewide. Processing times are expected to decrease due to new in-person options.

August 7, 2026 📅️

7.) Donna J. Jodhan – Changing Images at Airports | BarrierFreeCanada.org | August 7, 2026

Donna J. Jodhan describes how airports in Europe and the UK are adopting a broader set of accessibility symbols beyond the traditional wheelchair icon, including badges for vision, hearing, and mobility support. She argues that these visual updates foster better recognition of travelers’ diverse disabilities and encourage airport staff to provide more appropriate assistance. Jodhan calls for wider global adoption of these inclusive practices.

August 6, 2026 📅️

8.) Event: RESIST! Join the Launch of the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion: A LinkedIn Live Event | September 1, 2026 at 11AM PT | DrKirkAdams.com | August 6, 2026

The Institute for Sustainable Diversity & Inclusion (ISDI) will launch the Community Coalition for Sustainable Diversity and Inclusion via a LinkedIn Live event on September 1, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. PT. Dr. Kirk Adams and ISDI leaders invite participants from across sectors for an interactive Ask Us Anything session and to become Founding Members as DEIA programs face heightened national challenges.

9.) How Technology Helped a Deaf-Blind Man Fight His Disability | DeccanHerald.com | August 6, 2026

T Prabakaran, born with deafblindness in Andhra Pradesh, achieved independence using tools like Google Maps, Google Translate, OCR apps, and screen readers. Recognized with India’s National Award for Role Model for Persons with Multiple Disabilities in 2021, Prabakaran credits assistive technology for enabling autonomous travel, communication, and professional success.

10.) Trump Administration Moves Forward With Head Start Overhaul, Proposing to Eliminate Regulations | APNews.com | August 6, 2026

The Trump administration has proposed a major overhaul of the Head Start program, aiming to eliminate most federal regulations, including standards for staff-to-student ratios and mandatory wraparound services. Officials argue this would grant centers greater local flexibility and save over $2 billion, but advocates warn the changes threaten key supports for vulnerable children. New rules would require all instruction in English (with tribal exceptions) and cap administrative expenses at 5%.

11.) Civil Rights and Disability Organizations’ Joint Statement in Opposition to Administration Efforts to Dismantle Head Start | EdTrust.org | August 6, 2026

A coalition including EdTrust, the NAACP, and UnidosUS opposes the Trump administration’s proposal to overhaul Head Start, warning it would remove key quality standards, weaken support for children with disabilities, and increase barriers for families experiencing homelessness. The joint statement argues these changes would disproportionately harm Black, Latino, and disabled children.

12.) Courts to City Housing Depts: Pay for Accessibility Up Front–Or Pay More Later | ShelterForce.org | August 6, 2026

A federal settlement will compel Chicago to build or rehabilitate 2,800 accessible affordable housing units over 12 years and pay $2.25 million in damages after years of noncompliance with accessibility standards. Civil rights lawyers, including Michael Allen of Relman Colfax, warn that similar lawsuits could be imminent in 10 to 20 other US cities, given persistent enforcement gaps.

13.) As Federal Protections Fade, Disabled Americans Fear a Return to Institutions | Stateline.org | August 6, 2026

Federal policy shifts and funding cuts are threatening decades-old disability rights, with DOJ memos and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act prompting states to reduce community-based care. Advocates like Rob Stone and experts such as Alison Barkoff warn that millions with disabilities could lose support, risking forced institutionalization and reversing civil rights progress.

14.) Autism Diagnoses in NZ Have More Than Tripled Since 2009 | 1News.co.nz | August 6, 2026

A University of Otago study found New Zealand’s autism diagnoses more than tripled from 2009 to 2023, with prevalence increasing in both children and adults. By 2023, 1.3% of NZ children and 0.14% of adults had an autism diagnosis recorded. Lead researcher Ben Beaglehole said the ongoing rise highlights a need for greater capacity in health and disability services.

15.) Giannoulias Launches Pilot Program to Make Handicap Placards Easier to Obtain in Illinois | CBSNews.com | August 6, 2026

Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias has initiated a pilot program expanding access to parking disability placards, following a new law signed by Gov. JB Pritzker. Caregivers and legal guardians can now more easily obtain meter-exempt placards for individuals with disabilities who cannot drive. The program extends in-person services to 14 additional DMV locations for faster processing.

16.) Gillibrand Introduces Two Bills to Support Accessible Housing for Seniors and People With Disabilities | Gillibrand.senate.gov | August 6, 2026

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Senior Accessible Housing Tax Credit Act and the VITAL Act, aiming to improve accessible housing for seniors and people with disabilities. The first bill proposes a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $10,000 for essential home modifications for those aged 60 or older, while the VITAL Act would require at least 20% of Low-Income Housing Tax Credit units to be accessible and/or walkable.

17.) Promising Approaches for Keeping Our Seniors Housed and Healthy | Governing.com | August 6, 2026

States and localities face growing challenges as 12.4 million older households remain housing cost-burdened in the US. Sarah Rosen Wartell of the Urban Institute outlines targeted strategies including property tax circuit breakers, expanded ADU financing, and home modification grants to improve affordability and accessibility for seniors. Only 10 percent of US homes are currently accessible for older adults.

18.) Trump Administration Moves to Deregulate Head Start, Opening Door for Sweeping Change | NPR.org | August 6, 2026

The Trump administration has proposed major changes to Head Start, seeking to reduce federal standards and shift more control to states and parents. The plan would cut administrative spending caps from 15% to 5%, aiming to save $2.2 billion and increase spots for 200,000 more children. Advocates, including Yvette Sanchez Fuentes, caution these moves could compromise quality and access for vulnerable families.

19.) More Ohio Students Have a Disability: Schools, Families Face Challenges | SpringfieldNewsSun.com | August 6, 2026

Ohio public schools have seen the proportion of students with disabilities grow from 18% in 2020-21 to 20.4% in 2024-25, according to the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce. Administrators report rising costs, increased staffing needs, and funding challenges, while parents share mixed experiences seeking services. Voucher use, especially for autism, is also surging.

20.) Deaf Filmmaker Hopes International Award Is Just the Beginning | VillageReport.ca | August 6, 2026

Cambridge filmmaker Alvin Witcher won Best Feature Documentary at the Clin d’Oeil Festival in Reims, France, for “Gary Malkowski: A Deaf Legacy in Ontario.” The documentary chronicles Gary Malkowski, the first deaf MPP in Canada, and his impact on accessibility. Witcher hopes the international recognition will open more opportunities for deaf filmmakers and untold stories in Canada.

21.) New Kentucky Law Aims To Break Barriers for High School Graduates With Disabilities | WDRB.com | August 6, 2026

Kentucky will implement House Bill 562 starting with the 2027-28 school year, replacing the “certificate of completion” with a modified diploma for about 4,500 students with disabilities. Special education director Troy Kolb emphasized the new diploma will uphold rigorous standards and help graduates overcome employment barriers. Parents and advocates welcomed the bipartisan change.

August 5, 2026 📅️

22.) Away in August | DisabilityDebrief.org | August 5, 2026

Disability Debrief pauses publication in August as Peter Torres Fremlin takes a break in Berlin and works on editing eight upcoming contributor articles. These forthcoming stories will cover topics such as hearing voices in Argentina and examining disability in Rwanda’s precolonial history. Publication will resume in September.

23.) Welcome, Even Though I’m Blind: Why Our Newest Sponsor Named His Organization After His Own Song | AccessInformationNews.com | August 5, 2026

Cazerny Bussey, a Brooklyn-born recording artist, founded Even Though I’m Blind, Inc. (ETIB) in 2025, naming the organization after his own song. ETIB now runs a radio station, podcast, vetted business directory, and community initiatives led by blind individuals, emphasizing lived experience over pity. Access Information News announced ETIB as its newest sponsor, highlighting the group’s early but impactful efforts in blind-led media.

24.) Out of Sight and Out of Mind | Progressive.org | August 5, 2026

A recent DOJ memo asserts that neither the ADA nor the Supreme Court’s Olmstead decision require states to provide community-based support options for disabled people. Disability rights organizations, including the American Association of People with Disabilities and The Arc, warn that this stance could ease the path for states to revert to institutionalizing individuals with disabilities.

25.) The Accessibility Rules Were There. The Enforcement Wasn’t. | ShelterForce.org | August 5, 2026

Federal accessibility requirements for affordable housing have long existed, but attorney Michael Allen details how cities like Los Angeles and Chicago failed to enforce them, resulting in tens of thousands of inaccessible units. Landmark lawsuits forced LA and Chicago to settle, with LA committing to 4,000 accessible apartments and Chicago to 2,800, plus millions in damages. The rulings now set significant legal precedents for municipal housing oversight nationwide.

26.) No Ramp Out: The Payday Loan Hole of the Disability Community | TheCenturyFoundation.org | August 5, 2026

A 2025 survey commissioned by the Julian Bond Institute and Center for Responsible Lending found that roughly 1.6 million people with disabilities in the US use payday loans annually, losing over $860 million in fees. Kings Floyd details how predatory lending disproportionately impacts disabled Americans amid an affordability crisis, with regulatory gaps leaving millions at risk of financial exploitation.

27.) UK Airports Improve Accessibility as Demand for Assistance Services Reaches Record Levels | Thiis.co.uk | August 5, 2026

The UK Civil Aviation Authority’s 2025/26 Airport Accessibility Report shows 19 airports achieving a ‘very good’ rating and record demand for assistance services, with requests up 115.8 percent since 2015. Satisfaction among disabled passengers remains lower than the general public, and 58 percent still report difficulties, driving calls for further investment and regulatory powers.

28.) Are Saskatoon’s Crosswalk Signals Too Short? | CBC.ca | August 5, 2026

Some crosswalk signal times in Saskatoon fall short of national standards, raising accessibility concerns for people with mobility issues and children, according to advocacy group Strong Towns YXE. City engineering manager Nathalie Baudais says updates are underway but could take up to five more years as infrastructure projects take priority. Accessibility experts argue that improving signal timing benefits all residents.

29.) Congress Sets Today as the Deadline for DOJ Answers on Its Disability Care Opinion | MedicalDaily.com | August 5, 2026

One hundred members of Congress, led by Senators Dick Durbin, Tammy Duckworth, Ron Wyden, and Bernie Sanders, set August 5 as the deadline for the DOJ to respond to sharp criticism of its June legal opinion narrowing federal disability protections. While Olmstead v. L.C. remains in force, new DOJ guidance signals a shift in federal enforcement. Families’ current services remain unchanged, but advocates warn of potential risks for those relying on Medicaid-funded care.

30.) Can You Raise Children Without Screens Anymore? | Jessica Kellgren-Fozard | YouTube.com | August 5, 2026

Cutting through the hype around modern parenting, Jessica Kellgren-Fozard examines how families are navigating the realities of screens, algorithms, and digital education. She tackles questions on whether screen-free children are left behind, the complexities in schools’ approaches, and the rising need for critical digital literacy in an always-online world.

August 4, 2026 📅️

31.) Functional Vision Promotes Quality of Life and Socio-Emotional Functioning in Visually Impaired Children and Adolescents | Plos.org | August 4, 2026

A cross-sectional study of 91 visually impaired children and adolescents by Guido Catalano and colleagues found that higher levels of daily autonomy, as measured by the VIDA scale, are strongly associated with improved quality of life and fewer socio-emotional and behavioral problems. Functional vision, rather than visual acuity alone, was a key factor in psychological well-being in this population.

32.) Cart Aims To Give Disabled People Countryside Access | BBC.com | August 4, 2026

Simon Mulholland has developed the Obamobile, a horse-drawn cart designed for wheelchair users and people with limited mobility to access areas like the South Downs Way. The cart features an instant pony release system for safety, and has enabled thousands to visit previously unreachable countryside and beaches. Local authorities hope to expand similar services in Sussex.

33.) Nobody Is Talking About This Odyssey Controversy | Molly Burke | YouTube.com | August 4, 2026

Cutting through the hype around the Odyssey controversy, Molly Burke examines what recent developments actually reveal and why they matter for disability advocacy. With her firsthand experience navigating accessibility challenges, Molly offers insight into the community responses and what this debate signals for inclusive design.

August 3, 2026 📅️

34.) Trump Overhaul Could Gut Head Start Preschool Standards, Leaving States to Set the Rules | APNews.com | August 3, 2026

David also runs a weekly Tech Monday where people can chat about assistive and main stream technology, share information, and any tips and tricks.

David lost his sight when he was 8 years old and had to learn Braille. Since then, he completed high school, went to Sydney University receiving a Social Work degree, spent 4 years drug and alcohol counselling, and then moved into his current job.

As a person who is blind, David believes that as a user of the technology that he recommends to others, that he is well situated to look at the strengths and shortcomings of the assistive technology that he comes across in both his professional and personal life, in particular, mainstream technology that is accessible.

item.title: Welcome, Even Though I’m Blind: Why Our Newest Sponsor Named His Organization After His Own Song
item.dc:creator: Aaron Di Blasi
item.description:
Here, Aaron Di Blasi, Publisher for the Access Information News weekly newsletter, welcomes Cazerny Bussey and Even Though I'm Blind, Inc. (ETIB) as the publication's newest Sponsor, joining on August 10, 2026. Di Blasi opens with the detail that gives the piece its title: in 2021, Bussey, a Brooklyn-born recording artist who lost his eyesight at fifteen, released an album called Cfly 728, and one of its tracks was called "Even Though I'm Blind." Four years later, that song title is the name of an organization running an internet radio station, an interview podcast, a curated directory of blind-owned businesses, a blog, an events calendar, and a project that collects encouragement from the community in fifteen-second voice recordings. The introduction came from Dr. Kirk Adams in late July 2026; Bussey accepted the following morning, and his first note back thanked Adams before it thanked Di Blasi.
